speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext:
May
I direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I ask it in view of the uncertainty he expressed with regard to possible sales of wheat to Australia. I have in my hand the Australian Daily News, an official publication of the Australian government in North America, dated December 13, in which this official statement was made:
Minister for trade John McEwen said today Australia would import 1,500,000 bushels (60 lb. per bushel) of high-protein Canadian wheat for making certain types of bread in Sydney.
He also added:
If it became necessary, more Canadian wheat would be imported-
In view of that official statement of December 13, and the fact that there has been so much confusion on the part of the minister and in other quarters of the house, I wonder whether he has seen this statement before.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED PURCHASE OF 1,500,000 BUSHELS BY AUSTRALIA
speechtext: I do not think there is any confusion on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to this matter. The confusion has existed in the minds of my hon. friends.

maintopic: REPORTED PURCHASE OF 1,500,000 BUSHELS BY AUSTRALIA
speechtext: First of all the minister said he had not heard of such a suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED PURCHASE OF 1,500,000 BUSHELS BY AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
I do not recall having made such a statement whatsoever. I said I was fully aware of the situation in Australia with regard to their crop failure and the necessity they might have to import wheat if they wished to maintain their export markets. I also stated that there was no actual shortage of wheat in Australia to sustain their own population.
That would be borne out by the figures which you would find in the Wheat Review. I have the November issue in front of me, and the Australian supply position, as mentioned on page 29, indicates that they had total estimated supplies of 218 million bushels, with total exports of wheat and wheat flour of 92.6 million bushels, leaving a balance on November 3 for export and for carryover of 49.1 million bushels, a sufficient amount of wheat to sustain their population.
The problem facing Australia is to maintain its export position. As I understand the situation, they consider it perhaps advisable to import some Canadian wheat so they could export their Australian wheat to countries with which they have been dealing over the years. On the point as to whether or not it is essential for us to press upon the Australians the fact that we have wheat available for export, may I say that I pointed out yesterday that Australia has been in the wheat business for many years and is one of the four leading exporters of wheat, and that the Australian people in the wheat business are just as familiar with our situation as we are with theirs, because they get constant reports on the availability of supplies. We are prepared to do business with Australia; and the wheat board, I presume,

Inquiries of the Ministry has been in constant consultation with Australian officials. I do not see the difficulty which arises in the mind of my hon. friend.

maintopic: REPORTED PURCHASE OF 1,500,000 BUSHELS BY AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
May I ask a supplementary question of the minister. Does he not think in view of this statement that it would have been wise for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to have followed this up, or is he reverting to the policy of a former minister who said it was not the business of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to sell wheat?
I refer, of course, to Mr. Malcolm.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED PURCHASE OF 1,500,000 BUSHELS BY AUSTRALIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been spending a great deal of my time on the problem of how to advance the sale of Canadian wheat, and we are having considerable success in doing so. I am very much interested in the prospect for the sale of wheat to Australia, but I am naturally dependent upon information I receive from the wheat board. The wheat board meets daily, as my hon. friend knows, to consider possible sales, and they are not overlooking any opportunity to make sales of Canadian wheat.

The other course is an appeal on a question of law or jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Canada. There is no inconsistency in the position; there is no way the governor in council could anticipate what the railway companies might do.
The railway companies have given notice that they intend to apply for leave to appeal to a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. I am not going to place myself in the position of giving legal advice; naturally that would be improper. But I see no inconsistency in the position, nor any beclouding of the issues, for both situations are provided for in the statutes.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON PROGRESS OF FREIGHT EQUALIZATION INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Assiniboia asked me the following questions:
Could the minister inform the house as to when the board may be able to make another progress report representing another step forward? Second, is he able to ascertain what the board's target date is for completion of this very important inquiry?
Mr. Speaker, the board's program in the equalization of freight rates is such that it considers that another progress report could usefully be made before December, 1959, the board's target date for completion of its program of equalization. However, equalization of commodity rates, which are now being investigated, is subject to a variety of complicating factors, for many or most of them were established because of circumstances peculiar to each commodity and the territory in which they apply.
Hearings on due notice are also necessary in various cases in Canada in order to give affected parties an opportunity to be heard for, as was stated by the royal commission on transportation in 1951, many serious problems are involved; for example, the effects that equalization may have on railway revenues, on established industries, and on trade and market patterns, all of which are matters of the utmost importance.
The board can devote only a portion of its time to equalization, for its duty requires that it attend to a heavy volume of applications and complaints respecting matters other


than equalization. Factors beyond the control of the board may also make it impossible for the board to complete its program by the target date.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, January 8, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Ap-pelle)-Mr. Courtemanche in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with any of the Atlantic provinces to provide assistance in the generation of electric energy by thermal electric power projects and in the control and transmission of electric energy, and including provisions for the payment of a subvention on coal used in the production of electric energy.

Before the adjournment of this committee at ten o'clock last evening I said that officials of the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation were in Ottawa during the week of December 15, and that discussions took place at that time with officials of the Department of Public Works in connection with the future mining operations and the proposed harbour development at Caron Point site near Bathurst.
As the additional power that will be required in northern New Brunswick in the next decade will depend largely upon the extraction of metals from the concentrate by electro-metallurgical methods, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources or the Minister of Public Works should report to this committee on the results of the discussions which took place with officials of the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation. The people of Gloucester county and of New Brunswick have a right to know if the mineral discoveries and developments which have taken place in the northern section of the province during the last four years, and which will have a direct effect on the future requirements for electrical energy, are to be curtailed for an indefinite period. They also have a right to know what is contemplated by both federal and provincial authorities to assure that these developments will be carried on without delay to the best interest of the province and of the country in general.
In his statement when introducing this resolution the minister stated that for those Atlantic provinces which desire such aid, the dominion government would build and sell to the provinces such thermal plant and transmission facilities as may be agreed upon. Before this resolution is passed by the committee the minister should inform us as to the conditions and terms of such sales to the provinces concerned.
The minister stated that the amounts of money expended in the construction program will all be refunded with interest so that this phase of the program will be self-liquidating.


He should tell us what will be the depreciation on the thermal plants and on the transmission lines, and also if the interest charged is to be the same as mentioned for the Beech-wood project, that is, on the same basis as the long-term loans by the federal government.
With reference to the second phase of this resolution, we have a right to know what effect the estimated subvention of $1,700,000 per year will have on the cost of power as compared with present prices paid for coal purchased by the thermal plants now in operation in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The minister should also inform this committee how the cost of power or the price charged consumers after the coal subventions are applied will compare with power produced by thermal plants in central Canada, particularly in the province of Ontario.
The minister should also clarify the comments made by the premier of New Brunswick to the effect that the method of financing power development, as outlined in the secret memorandum which represented Conservative policy on power development and which has been refused to us, entailed rates of interest considerably in excess of anything proposed to date by the government of Canada to the government of New Brunswick. We also have a right to clarification of another comment by the premier of New Brunswick to the effect that the memorandum does not conform to the principles which have been discussed over the last six months by representatives of the government of Canada and of the governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, to which I referred in my remarks last evening.
In the case of generating plants, will the annual payment be based on the federal longterm rate of interest plus the sum required to amortize the plant in 30 years, and in the case of transmission lines will the annual payment be based on the same rate of interest plus the sum required to amortize the lines in 40 years?

Mr. Chairman, before this resolution carries I would like to make one or two comments. The wording of the resolution makes it apply to the Atlantic provinces, and for that reason it has a regional application. The use of the word "thermal" in the third line makes this resolution discriminative against Newfoundland, which is one of the Atlantic provinces, because the accepted interpretation of a thermal electric power project is a power plant where electricity is generated from heat derived from the use of coal.
In Newfoundland k is impossible for us to benefit from this resolution because we do not have any local coal resources that may be utilized in this way. We have to depend on Nova Scotia for our coal, and the supply

from which we have been drawing in Nova Scotia has been getting shorter and more difficult to obtain as the years have gone by.
The use of this coal in the Atlantic provinces-Nova Scotia and other maritime provinces-for thermal plants would possibly have a harmful effect on our coal supplies in Newfoundland; the increased demand would make our coal either scarcer or higher in price.
On the other hand, we do have in Newfoundland, and particularly in my own riding, undeveloped sources of hydroelectric power which could very well come within the scope of this resolution if the word "thermal" were not included. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that though using the word "thermal" the resolution does not specify from what source the heat is to be derived. It could be derived from coal, but it could also be derived from thermonuclear energy. It is just a matter of the source of the heat.
For this reason we would prefer to see this resolution amended by having the word "thermal" at the end of line 3 deleted. If this were done we believe it would not do any harm to any other of the Atlantic provinces, but it would be bringing Newfoundland within the scope of this resolution. At the present time Newfoundland is excluded from any benefit under the proposal.

Mr. Chairman, the terms of this resolution refer to the Atlantic provinces, and I think it is generally accepted that the Atlantic provinces include New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. So I think nobody could have any disagreement about providing more and cheaper electric power for the maritime provinces, and if this project is going to be undertaken I think it is reasonable to assume that in the development of this additional electric power the resources within a province, whatever they may be, will be used.
If we were to look through the figures with regard to electric power available from water sources as supplied by the minister's department, we should note that the power available from water sources in Newfoundland is four times as great as that available in the other three maritime provinces combined. In Newfoundland at the moment the turbine installation is capable of generating
329.000	horsepower, which is approximately
240.000	kilowatts, and this is almost equal to the total turbine installations of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island combined.
Now it may be true, and I think it is, that if the supply of electric power in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward 96698-1944
Atlantic Provinces Power Development Island is to be increased, there is a good deal to be said in favour of the source of energy being some type of thermal plant, because of the fact that there is not sufficient power from water available in those three provinces. We in Newfoundland are not in that position; and it appears to me that under the terms of this resolution as it is now drafted, if the word "thermal" is used we will be ruled out, in the sense that in increasing the electric supply in Newfoundland it would be better to use water power than to use energy supplied by heat. If we were to use energy supplied by heat we should need to import coal or oil into the province.
In these circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I propose to move an amendment to this resolution. My amendment is seconded by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, and reads as follows:
That the word "thermal", the last word in line 3 of the resolution, be deleted from the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether I have before me an exact copy of the amendment which was moved, but I understand that it deletes the word "thermal" in the third line of the resolution. May I point out that by doing that it obviously broadens the terms of the resolution and would in consequence impose an additional expenditure on the government of the day. An amendment of this kind could only be brought in by the government in the usual way in which amendments bringing about the expenditure of moneys is done, and obviously an amendment of this type is out of order when brought in by a private member.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to address myself to the point of order raised by the Minister of Public Works in his capacity as leader of the house. I quite agree with the general proposition that an amendment to a resolution preceding a money bill can only be made by the government after a message from the crown. That is the well accepted and very proper rule which I would certainly never question or challenge.
But if I may, sir, I am going to quote the words that were used by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in his presentation of this resolution last evening, as recorded at page 3038 of Hansard, in an endeavour to convince you that this particular amendment does not in any way increase any charge upon the crown. The third full paragraph of the minister's remarks on that page reads as follows:
Perhaps I should make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that the legislation to be introduced under the terms of this resolution will not in itself appropriate or authorize the expenditure of any sums

It therefore seems to me that since this amendment would not impose any charge on the government but would only empower it to extend this policy to plants that were not thermal plants, if the government saw fit to do so, the amendment should be accepted. speechtext: -which have to be introduced by resolutions could be amended by private members, and that argument is utterly fallacious.

speechtext:
The Minister of Northern
Affairs and National Resources was quite correct when he said that in itself the resolution does not appropriate any money. That is perfectly right. I think the majority of resolutions that are brought in do not provide for the actual appropriation of a specified sum of money. The very fact that this resolution itself could be brought in only after it had been placed before His Excellency and then had to be brought in in the form of a resolution indicates that the measure is one that can be amended only by the government.
The argument submitted by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate may be a very good one on which to hang a political argument, and I think that is all that was intended by the hon. member as demonstrated by his remarks-

It has some value, it is true. Just before the adjournment the minister told us we would benefit in connection with any transmission lines which might be built. Well, there are places in Newfoundland and in my riding which need electric power, and we should be very grateful if the government would give us an assurance that this resolution would include any transmission lines which the government may wish to build. But from the standpoint of thermal power this does not help us, because although we have some deposits of coal they are not of such economic value as to enable us to generate electricity.
On the other hand, we have an abundance of hydro power; a great abundance, not only on the island of Newfoundland itself but in that part of Labrador which belongs to my province. One of the greatest potential hydroelectric developments in the world is in the Grant Falls on the Hamilton river. A couple of years ago I went into this question while I was on the committee on research, and the potential was said to be at least six million horsepower, a capacity which could quite possibly be doubled in the course of time. The problem is, of course, to develop that sort of energy and to find a use for the power. We also have in Newfoundland itself undeveloped hydro power at Bay d'Espoir on the southwest coast and other places.
So if the words "hydroelectric power" are not included in the resolution, and if we are confined to thermo-electric power, the province of Newfoundland cannot participate fully in the intent of this resolution; and of course we should like our province to be able to do this. Although we will probably derive some minor advantages from the resolution I believe, as I indicated, that the government in drawing up this resolution and using the phrase "Atlantic provinces" fully intended that Newfoundland should participate fully. It is for that reason, I think, that the premier of Newfoundland sent his telegram to the minister pointing out the difficulty.
I have no desire to hinder the passing of the resolution, and no desire to do anything which would delay the benefits which may arise under this resolution for New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. But I do say it is unfortunate that the minister, who evidently does not understand Newfoundland affairs as well as we would

like him to do-and I do not say that is his fault-has not made better provision for the interests of the province from which 1 come.
There is a way out. I could move an amendment but you, Mr. Chairman, would probably object. The Minister of Finance objected this morning to an amendment proposed by another hon. member on this side of the house on the ground that it would probably add to the expenditure of the government. Now I am going to say that I believe the government is sincere in its proposals embodied in this resolution, and I hope for that reason the minister will take into consideration the suggestion I am about to make. If he would add, after "thermal" the words "and hydroelectric power projects" I think that would solve our problem in Newfoundland and enlarge the scope of the resolution so we could participate fully in its intent. The relevant part of the resolution would then read, "... . Atlantic provinces to provide assistance in the generation of electric power by thermal and hydroelectric power projects."
I ask the minister to take this into consideration. I cannot move an amendment on these lines myself; that could only be done by a member of the government. So I ask the minister in all sincerity to take this suggestion into consideration and embody in the resolution the words I have suggested.
In my opinion this would end all the discussion we have had in this committee today, clarify the situation as far as Newfoundland is concerned and, I think, satisfy all who are connected with this problem. If the minister could at some time this afternoon or on another early occasion take action on the lines I have indicated I think it would be very acceptable to the house.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution under discussion today to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with any of the Atlantic provinces to provide assistance in the generation of electric energy by thermal electric power projects is of very considerable interest to the province of Prince Edward Island. The cost of electric power in our province is extremely high, probably higher than in any other province, and higher than the rates charged in many lands.
When one considers the topography of our island, the reasons are obvious. Our countryside is low and rolling, with little water potential and no natural basins or storage facilities of any size. We have no coal, and to date we have no oil resources. At the present time surveys and boring operations are in progress and we are hopeful that the

results may be good, but we cannot depend on anything in this line for the present, at least.
That leaves us with the alternative of either importing coal or oil as fuel or transporting electrical energy into the province. The latter proposal would entail combating the high energy loss sustained by underwater cable. The former proposition, that of importing coal, is possibly now a feasible project with the coal subventions which might be paid by this government.
In this regard I would draw the attention of the government to a plan discussed in our area not many years ago. The proposition was to transport coal from western Cape Breton or from the Pictou area by barge to the large port of Georgetown on the eastern coast of Prince Edward Island, where an electrical plant could be set up at waterside. The coal would be taken from pithead to barge by escalator, transported at a very cheap water rate and taken from the barge by escalator right into the plant. This is a suggestion worthy of consideration, and I strongly urge that all the possibilities of this plan be studied. This is especially pertinent in view of the assistance by way of coal subventions which I have just mentioned, and should also provide the coal industry in the Atlantic provinces with considerable assistance.
For years the people of our area have asked for arrangements by way of assistance in providing cheaper electrical power. As in the case of many of our other submissions, we could not get any degree of sympathy for the Atlantic provinces' problems from the previous government. It has been the pledge of our party for the past three elections that we would provide such assistance, and now it is being done. We are pleased and most appreciative that recognition of this and other problems peculiar to the Atlantic provinces has been accorded to us.
This has been another of the milestones achieved under the Diefenbaker government in the development of national policy, a recognition of the particular needs of some areas, a realization that if we are to have a strong and united country we must be fair and wise in the development of every part of it. We cannot leave that development to take place in a willy-nilly fashion to the benefit of the central areas and to the detriment of the outer areas such as has happened in the last two decades.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I would like to add my remarks to those of hon. members who have spoken in favour of this resolution. Many of the remarks placed on the record with regard to the previous resolution under
Atlantic Provinces Power Development order No. 9 on the order paper might be pertinent to this one. Above all we do appreciate the new principle being put into effect with regard to the eastern provinces. Under this resolution the government has placed the opportunity before any of the Atlantic provinces. I do not know what the attitude of our local government will be toward entering into an agreement, but I hope it will give every consideration to the provisions of this resolution. If such an agreement would give our province relief from the high rates we now have to pay for electrical energy it would be most welcome, and I give my wholehearted support to this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I have some remarks I should like to make at this time, but before doing so I have one or two questions I wish to direct to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and I would hope that he might be able to answer them immediately. I would like to know if the agreements that are contemplated by this resolution are in fact either in the process of being signed or have been signed, and whether under those agreements the provinces involved have agreed on completion of the power plants to buy them and, if so, over what period of time the provincial governments or their power commissions may pay for the plants or transmission lines?

I appreciate receiving that information from the minister, Mr. Chairman. As has already been indicated, we in this group are quite happy to support the resolution, believing that it is an important step forward and that it will help a deficit power area in the country.
It does seem to me, however, that the terms of the resolution would have been much more acceptable to the nation as a whole if they had been somewhat different. I am not able to understand the thinking of the government in confining this policy at this time to the Atlantic provinces. I fail to see why in the resolution as it now stands the word "Atlantic" should appear at all. The government has said, the minister has said and the Prime Minister has said that there is or will be an over-all power policy for Canada. If that is the case I can see no reason why this resolution should include the word "Atlantic", which will mean that if this type of policy is to be extended at some later date to other parts of the country new legislation will be required, a new motion, new approval by parliament.
I can think of no other hon. member of the cabinet who has taken more interest in power over the years than has the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. He has travelled across his own province pointing out the great need for power in that area, and it seems strange indeed that in introducing this legislation, the first brought in by this government to deal with power, the province of Saskatchewan from which the minister comes would have been omitted from the resolution.
No one can say that the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia do not require some assistance. I think it could be readily proven that these are depressed areas as far as power is concerned; but no matter what yardstick is used to determine whether those
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

provinces are depressed in regard to power I believe the same yardstick will show that other provinces in this country also have a good claim for this type of assistance from the government.
I hold in my hand statistics which were supplied by the Saskatchewan Power Corporation. They relate to power needs and power facilities in various provinces of this country. They point out that in Nova Scotia there are 27 power outlets per 100 of population; in New Brunswick, 26 per 100; in British Columbia, 31 per 100; and in Saskatchewan just 24 per 100. On the basis of those figures alone I suggest that a province like Saskatchewan should have as good a claim for the same consideration under this legislation as has the province of New Brunswick or the province of Nova Scotia.
I tell the minister that the terms of repayment he has outlined, namely 30 years for power plants and 40 years for transmission lines, are good terms. I think the length of time for repayment is reasonable. I do not think anyone can quarrel with those provisions; but I can tell him, and I think he is already aware of it, that these are precisely the same kind of terms and the same kind of conditions for the building of thermal plants as are required in the province from which he comes. A burden is now being placed on the treasury of that province for expansion in the field of power which makes it a question mark whether the province can meet the power needs of the people in that area in the future.
Therefore I am suggesting to the minister and the government that this legislation, precisely because it is good legislation, should not be confined to the Atlantic provinces. If the government has a national policy-and some of us are wondering whether it is a national policy at all or rather a catch as catch can policy, or a political policy which is geared to what appears to be the best interests of the government party at the moment-how in the world can it be called a national policy when you have legislation dealing with only one section of the country?
Over the years in this house I have not taken the attitude I have seen some other hon. members take, that because something does not provide any particular benefit at the moment for their area or for their province they vote against it. I think that is a narrowminded and parochial attitude. I do not think it accomplishes anything. I welcome this legislation without reservation, but because I think it is good legislation I suggest the government has made a very grave error in confining the terms of the resolution to the Atlantic provinces. As a matter of fact I could present other information to show

that in certain ways some other parts of Canada have a more difficult power problem than have the provinces to which this legislation applies.
I am informed that on the average it takes 5 miles of power line to service 100 customers in Nova Scotia. In New Brunswick it takes 6 miles of power line to service 100 customers. In British Columbia it takes 3 miles of power line to service 100 customers, but in Saskatchewan it takes 16 miles of power line to service 100 customers. It takes three times as much power line to service a given number of customers in Saskatchewan as it does in either Nova Scotia or New Brunswick; yet by the terms of this resolution Saskatchewan is excluded.
I should like the minister to disclose the government program for the other provinces. Saskatchewan finds that because of the scattered area of settlement, it has a very difficult power problem. Not only that, but it finds that its need for power is growing now at the rate of 20 per cent per year, so that the need for power facilities and power output doubles every four years in that province. Just last year Saskatchewan had to raise $60 million for power. It will soon have raised $150 million for the distribution of power.
I suggest to the minister, and I think he knows this very well, that Saskatchewan today faces a power crisis and has a claim on this government for the same kind of terms and the same type of policy as are provided to the other provinces. I can say that Saskatchewan would certainly welcome any program of the federal government under which this government would build thermal plants and then sell them to the province, amortized over a period of 30 years, with the payment for power lines over a period of 40 years.
I am informed that in Nova Scotia there are 10,000 miles of transmission and distribution lines; in New Brunswick, 9,000 miles of transmission and distribution lines; in British Columbia, 14,000 miles of transmission and distribution lines; but in Saskatchewan, 34,000 miles of power lines. In other words the province of Saskatchewan has more than three times as many miles of power lines as has Nova Scotia and almost four times as many as New Brunswick. It means that we have to take power to a widely scattered population over a tremendous area, which makes our cost of distribution very high per customer.
I have some other statistics to show the population of farming area per square mile. In Nova Scotia the population of farming area per square mile is 23; in New Brunswick it is 28, and in Saskatchewan it is

I believe I could best answer the minister by saying that I do not complain about what is being done for the Atlantic provinces. The Atlantic provinces have not obtained from confederation the same kind of economic standards and the same policies that have applied to other parts of this country. I believe the Atlantic provinces have a good claim for such legislation. All I am doing is submitting to the government that the province from which the minister and I come has a claim that is, at least in many respects, equal to the claim of the Atlantic provinces. I am saying that what is a good policy for the maritime provinces is a good policy for the prairie provinces. I see no reason why the government should have one policy today for the Atlantic provinces, and not be in a position to announce its policy for the other provinces in this country.
I should like to know from the minister what discussions are taking place toward arriving at this national policy to which he has referred. I want to know where a province like Saskatchewan is going to stand with the government in getting the same kind of offer, particularly when there is to be no immediate resumption of the federal-provincial conference and that avenue, at least, will not be open for such discussions. I do appeal to the minister and to the government to come forward with the national power policy they promised the people of this country, and not rest content with a policy that applies only to one part of this nation.

I wish at the very beginning of my remarks to indicate my wholehearted support for this particular measure, which is likely to have very important consequences for the province of Nova Scotia. I believe the fact that this measure has come before the house reflects the widespread feeling, not only amongst members of the house but also in the country, that special measures are required in order to advance the economic welfare of the Atlantic region. I realize that one of the main objects of this resolution is to permit the more rapid industrial expansion of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
It should, however, be stated that access to power is only one of the factors in economic development. It is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for economic development. It would be a mistake, in supporting this resolution, to put forward the idea to the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick that this


is the final solution to the problems of that area. The cost of power is important in industrial development only in so far as it affects the cost of production. In certain industries the cost of power is a minor factor in production, but in other industries it is an overwhelming factor. However, this is a very important step forward and it has the support of the people of Nova Scotia.
We know, Mr. Chairman, that the problem of power has been raised in this house before, and its application to the Atlantic provinces. As a matter of fact, just about two years ago there was an amendment to a motion to go into supply upon which the problem of power was discussed for two days, with respect not only to the maritimes but to all parts of Canada. The views that were expressed on that occasion have some application to the diagnosis that has been given by the minister as to the crux of the power problem in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
On two occasions, last night and again today, the minister has stated that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were power short or power deficit areas. I should like the minister to elaborate further on this particular diagnosis of the problem, because it does not coincide fully with other views that were expressed in that debate on power to which I have referred. When the former member for Cape Breton South took part in that debate he had this to say:
The discussion would suggest that the development of Nova Scotia was retarded because of the lack of power. It is not true that there is lack of power. There is now developed in Nova Scotia power that could be used by any industry that may come in there.
I had occasion during the same debate to refer to an interim study that had been made by the power committee of the Atlantic provinces economic council of power problems in that area. I quoted the remarks made by Mr. Tweeddale, assistant chief engineer of the New Brunswick power commission. He said that basically there is an adequate supply of electrical power available in the maritime regions to meet present demands. The committee believes that electric power can be made available to any section of the region to meet future demands. This interpretation, of course, is somewhat at variance with the diagnosis of the minister. I must at the same time, however, concede that there is in Nova Scotia, and in New Brunswick as well, a feeling that these areas are power short.
I have here the report of an address given four years ago at St. Francis Xavier University by a businessman, Mr. Dyson Crowe, who spoke as follows:
I'm not alone in advocating government owned cheap electricity as the fundamental answer to our Nova Scotian and maritime problems. This is the

common and universal answer of all who have ever studied the question. Just a few nights ago at the fishermen's convention in Amherst, Dr. M. M. Coady, of your extension department, advocated this very thing as the fundamental answer to maritime disabilities.
Hence the minister is not alone in his view although, after having discussed the matter on occasion with the officials of the Nova Scotia power commission in particular, I believe the problem is not so much the difficulty of generating a supply of electricity, but that the difficulty is to generate a supply of electricity at a price comparable with costs in central Canada. This same power committee of the Atlantic provinces economic council stated that the power rates in the Atlantic region were comparable to the power rates on the eastern seaboard of the United States. I should be happy if the minister would assist my understanding and that of the public of the nature of the problem we are now attempting to solve by throwing further light on this particular matter, as to whether the real problem is a power deficit or the need to generate greater quantities of electricity at lower rates.
With that preliminary view, I certainly felt that the minister in introducing this resolution last night was in a very enviable position, because as his first task as a minister in this house he had the privilege of introducing a measure that has been long sought and is now a reality through this resolution. The satisfaction he felt, I am sure, was sincere, although I must confess that I felt that the remarks of the minister last night and today were tinged somewhat by selfdelusion; because he attempted to convey the impression, or at least let me say that he left the impression with me, that he had come to his task as Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and that no plans were in the files, no discussions had preceded his accession to office, and that he himself had decided from the very beginning to develop a power program for the maritime provinces.
When the former minister of northern affairs and national resources last night attempted to stake out a claim, which I thought was a modest one in the circumstances, for a share of the credit for these power proposals, his statement was met by explosions of disbelief on the part of members on the government side of the house. Because this is a good measure, I think I will attempt to set out today the Liberal contribution to this particular problem, or the Liberal stage of development and then, I hope, fairly assess what I consider to be the additional embellishments or improvements that have been made since June 10 or the accession of the new government.
Atlantic Provinces Power Development
The very inspiration for the thinking behind this proposal came from an extremely important report made in 1954 by Professor Christie of Johns Hopkins University. Professor Christie had been asked by the dominion coal board to investigate the problem of the generation of electricity from thermal sources in the maritime provinces, not only in order to meet the situation in respect to electricity but also to provide further markets for coal from that area. On previous occasions I have referred to this report which was submitted on September 20, 1954, to the dominion coal board, and which is entitled, "Thermal Power from, Canadian Coal: The Maritime Situation". As I listened to the minister last night expose the advantages of this plan I could not but recall the words which Professor Christie used in this report. He states:
To ultimately attain minimum electrical rates in the maritime provinces, it is proposed that New Brunswick and Nova Scotia be considered a single area for electrical generation and distribution.
That is the essence of the plan and on the following page, namely page 9, he lists I believe ten advantages that would accrue from this integration. Among these were the very advantages that were pointed out by the minister last night:
(a) The combined system would justify the installation of large steam turbine units built for the maximum fuel economy and which could serve with run of river plants as base load units.
And again:
(e) Such large units on an interconnected system would reduce the cost of reserves, which each utility in the system would otherwise have to maintain for emergency purposes.
And finally:
(g) The addition of low cost capacity to hydro storage plants would lessen the cost of serving peak loads.
In the plan elucidated by the minister last night there is nothing which was not first proposed in this report. I certainly do not think there is anything wrong with that, except that it should be pointed out that the dominion coal board, as an agency of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, had first provided the opportunity for a plan of this kind. I believe this particular work of the dominion coal board is one of the real contributions they have made to this country. It was not unusual that following the presentation of this report it was referred to and put forward as a basis for a plan in this House of Commons on a number of occasions.
I personally felt a great sense of satisfaction when Mr. Harris, in his budget address of last spring, brought together the ideas of Professor Christie and announced them as government policy. I felt that here had been
3076	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development a realization that the needs of the maritime provinces were legitimate needs, and that the government of the day, with the support of the House of Commons, was prepared to put forward a plan that would do the work that was required. Just for the record, Mr. Chairman, may I quote one or two sentences from the budget address of Mr. Harris. He states, as reported at page 2,220 of Hansard:
Such interconnection would reduce the requirements for stand-by capacity and would permit the most advantageous location of thermal plants and the building of larger and more efficient thermal units.
Then again:
Under this proposal, the transmission lines would be rented on a non-profit basis and the power would be sold at cost to provincial electric systems. The purpose would be that the plants and other facilities built under this program can be acquired by the provinces at any time on payment of their amortized cost.
The next step in the elaboration of this power plan occurred on April 9, 1957, when the then minister of northern affairs and national resources, made a very important statement to the House of Commons telling us the state of the negotiations between the provinces and the federal government, and announcing to us that in principle the provinces had accepted the federal offer.
That was a very important step forward, but I want to refer in particular to one paragraph of this statement where the then minister pointed out that the Montreal Engineering Company had been retained by the Northern Canada Power Commission to undertake engineering studies, the purpose of such studies being to ascertain where these plants should be built and the effect which the development of larger thermal units and an interconnected system would have on the cost of electricity in the maritime provinces. In other words the broad plan had been laid before the House of Commons by Mr. Harris and the former minister, and the engineering and practical aspects were to be worked out by this Montreal Engineering Company.
At that time it was expected that the report of the Monteral Engineering Company would be available by August 1, and likely it was. That is why, Mr. Chairman, the present Prime Minister was able to say things about power which the former prime minister was not able to say; because he was able, as a result of these studies, to indicate to the house and to the country the extent to which power costs would be reduced by means of this particular innovation.
I am conscious of the fact that in Fredericton the prime minister of the day followed the only wise and responsible course in telling


the people there that he could not say by how much power costs would be reduced, pending completion of the reports; although with one exception the elements upon which the minister elaborated last night, which elements would reduce the power costs, were present in the plan as presented to this house last March and April.
I remember that earlier the Prime Minister, in referring in this house to the power plan, said that the Liberal party had served up a dish which was unpalatable and that the Tory government had served up a dish which would be palatable. Well, I suppose the best judges of the palatability of the dish would be the people of Nova Scotia, and when this initial plan was put forward by the Liberal government it had an immediate response from the people of that province. I have in my hand an editorial in the Halifax Chronicle Herald dated March 25 with the caption "Giant Project", with reference to the Liberal power plan, which says that the probable magnitude of the federal government's planned power development in the maritime provinces, as disclosed by the initial blueprints, is something much larger than most citizens of this area had anticipated.
Another editorial some weeks later entitled "Forging Ahead" says "The announcement by resources minister Jean Lesage of plans for immediate construction of the first of the new federally owned thermal plants in the maritimes is the result of the most heartening display of intergovernmental cooperation in a long time."
The Antigonish Casket said in an editorial entitled "Boosting Maritime Power": "This is wonderful news for the maritime provinces and the most promising development. It is definite proof of concern on the part of the federal authorities for the eastern provinces and their inability to keep in step with the industrial growth of the nation. It supports the point of view held by so many of our leaders that a key factor to industrial progress in our region is economic and sufficient power. It may well be-" decided the observer who, by the way, is one of the keenest students in Nova Scotia "-that this report of minister Lesage will trigger a resurgence of industrial activity in these maritime provinces."
May I now refer to further authorities. I have with me statements in the Halifax Chronicle Herald of March 16 under the headline "Province Welcomes Budget News".
"Anything which will lead to cheaper industrial power in this region is most welcome", Premier Stanfield said yesterday.

Later in the same story the united mine workers had this to say:
District 26 united mine workers of America welcomes a thermal power program set forth in the budget address of Hon. Walter Harris.
The public response in Nova Scotia to this program as outlined by Mr. Harris and Mr. Lesage in the House of Commons was warm, and may I conclude my recitation of authorities by referring to a one-page advertisement in the Halifax Chronicle Herald by the Conservative party in Nova Scotia. It states, "The question of federal thermal power proposals is not an issue". So they too, apparently, found this dish palatable, because they did not want to make it an issue in the election in the province of Nova Scotia.
Mr. Chairman, my reason for setting out this summary of evidence is simple and clear. The minister has left the impression that this plan before the house was developed ab initio by his government at the request of two provinces. This was an inherited plan. It has been added to in one important particular, a particular which was inherent in the plan which would have been the outcome of commitments which had been made by the previous government. I refer to the decision of the government to apply a subvention on the movement of coal to these maritime plants.
I believe there has been a great deal of confusion as to the stand of the previous government on this particular matter. Full guarantees were given that coal would be used in these plants. The new government has now added a further embellishment or improvement to the plan which was ready for them when they came into office.

That is the point, and it is one which has obviously escaped the attention of many people. As the minister knows, this is another key point-the studies which were then being made by the Montreal Engineering Company.
A subvention on the movement of coal is assistance in the development of electric power. The word "subvention" has been used in the past to describe those payments which were made for the movement of maritime coal to meet the competition of United States coal in central Canada. This new application of the subvention is an ingenious one, but it is not precisely the same application and it does not fall within the usual definition of a subvention. It will add to the attractiveness of this power program for the maritime provinces, but I say it would be unusual if a new government of Canada, such as the one now holding office, could not find a way to make some additional improvements in a plan which was, in its entirety, so important and so useful to the economy of Nova Scotia. The response of the Liberal government to the needs and the power possibilities of the maritime provinces was a massive response. The response of the new Tory government is an agonizing reacceptance of the Liberal policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The people did not think so.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking to this resolution I must say I am delighted that the government has recognized the needs of the Atlantic provinces, particularly since I understand that the Atlantic provinces have been in a period of depression, or recession, for some years past, due largely to capital Liberal policy, or the policy of former governments, though I do not wish to pursue the question of who is to blame for this state of affairs which has made this legislation necessary. That is not my purpose at this time. I just want to ask the minister one or two questions, and I will come to them shortly.
The resolution as it stands-and I will not read it in its entirety-provides for the government to assist in the generation of electric energy by thermal electric power projects and in the control and transmission of electric energy, including provisions for the payment of a subvention on coal used in the production of electric energy. It specifically mentions the Atlantic provinces. One of the hon. members who spoke earlier in the debate, and possibly others as well, wondered at the time why this was not declared to be a national policy. I, likewise, wonder why the word "Atlantic" was inserted in the
3078	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development resolution as it now stands, because certainly there are other parts of Canada which could well make use of this type of legislation, including the province of British Columbia. I know that we have great resources of water power available. However, the minister himself must be aware that the capital cost of providing equipment for the proper development of these power resources is becoming prohibitive, and that it is increasingly difficult to raise the hundreds of millions of dollars necessary for such development, and to do this on an economic basis.
The minister did give me some hope, because he had this to say as recorded in Hansard on page 3038:
Given electric energy at a cost competitive with that available in other areas of Canada the people in the Atlantic region will be in a much better position to compete successfully with all comers in Canada or elsewhere.
And again on page 3039 he expresses himself in these terms:
The subvention on coal for power production based on such a differential and paid on performance should, firstly, give the Atlantic provinces an opportunity of competing more successfully with the rest of Canada from the viewpoint of power costs.
Those two quotations would in themselves indicate that the cost of power throughout the various provinces of Canada has been carefully studied, and that it has been found that the cost in the Atlantic provinces is high as compared with the cost in other provinces; to such an extent, indeed, as to make it necessary for the government to provide a subvention on coal used for the development of power in that region.
I would ask the minister, therefore, to indicate to the committee-I am not questioning his statement in any way, but I should just like to know

what the various provinces pay for power so that we can give this matter the thorough study which I think it deserves.
On page 3039 the minister continues:
Secondly, there will be an indirect support for the Atlantic seaboard coal to be used in this region.
I may say in respect of that that we have coal mines in my province which have been idle for some years and which might become productive again if we had the opportunity to develop power by means of a subvention, on the same basis as is provided in this resolution. An arrangement of this sort would enable us to have the power which we so badly require.
Lest any members of the committee be under the impression that there is unlimited hydro power to spare in British Columbia,
I would draw to their attention the fact


that we are building a thermal plant at loco at the cost of many millions of dollars-a hundred million dollars estimate-the purpose of which is to make electric power available on the lower mainland at a price which would compete with the supposedly cheap waterpower we are said to enjoy at this time. For this reason it seems to me that the minister should outline specifically any reasons why he should oppose the striking out of the word "Atlantic" in his resolution, so that it would read as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with any of the provinces to provide assistance in the generation of electric energy by thermal electric power projects and in the control and transmission of electric energy, and including provisions for the payment of a subvention on coal used in the production of electric energy.
On this basis I feel it would be a more desirable and palatable resolution than as it now stands. Certainly I concede and I am satisfied that the people in my province and throughout Canada as a whole join me in welcoming the fact that the Atlantic region will receive the preference at this time because of its depressed condition but we would like to see legislation introduced that would make it possible to extend assistance of this kind to every province in Canada requiring it without the necessity of having to go to parliament to bring in an amendment to the act.
As I said earlier, the cost of electrical power throughout the nation should be studied. I believe we should know what we are talking about when we speak of cheaper power for the Atlantic provinces as compared with the other provinces so we can rest assured that the money we are being asked to expend today for this project will achieve the desired results.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is with a great deal of pride and pleasure that I rise to speak in support of this resolution. The pride arises out of the fact that it is a Conservative government led by the great and illustrious Prime Minister, champion of the little man in Canada, which has introduced this legislation. At long last we in Nova Scotia and the Atlantic provinces have been discovered by Ottawa and it has taken a Conservative government to make this discovery. In line with this it has had the courage and imagination to do something of value for this part of Canada. Of course, I could say that we were "discovered" once again by the previous government, just prior to the last election as we had been on similar occasions for many years, but that was as far as it ever went. In fact, just before the

last election we were promised everything under the sun short of moving the national capital from Ottawa to Halifax.
By John Diefenbaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
We were deluged with cabinet ministers in their eleventh hour repentance; and after all the deadwood had been brought in they tried their luck with "smallwood" but alas the people of Nova Scotia were not going to be fooled again. As one prominent newspaper has stated:
The Conservative government is being true, not only to its election promises, but to its whole concept of national development, when it announces large-scale measures to promote production and distribution of cheap power in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
I feel that the announcement of this program is to be highly commended. It offers the type of assistance specifically directed toward industrial growth that will do the maritimes the most good. For generations we have lagged behind the rest of Canada in progress and prosperity. In 1956, for example, Nova Scotia's per capita income was $1,000 and New Brunswick's $923 against a national average of $1,350. It may be said that the Atlantic provinces are being specially favoured by this government. This is not so. We have not been asking for favours, only for our rights, and it has taken a Conservative government to recognize them. I think all hon. members must have heard at one time or another of maritime rights. This is the boldest step ever taken by any government since confederation to raise the economy of this area.
The rash of promises that were made by the former government in its dying throes prior to the last election made mention of the construction of thermal plants but there is a tremendous difference in the proposal made at that time and the excellent one we have before us now. By a strange coincidence that death-bed proposal was made on March 14 by some fellow by the name of Harris. Every one in the opposition is talking about that date. How interesting that it should have been made on March 14, 1957, and then came June 10, 1957. What a strange coincidence. I do not know what the connection is between these two dates but they are separated by only a short space of time.
I was pleased to note when the Prime Minister made his momentous announcement in this house on November 14 last concerning assistance to the Atlantic provinces, the Leader of the Opposition was quick to see the difference to which I have referred. In his remarks one of the chief differences he
Atlantic Provinces Power Development noted was that this government was prepared to pay subventions on coal used for power purposes. He indicated that this would probably have the double-barrelled effect of aiding the coal industry as well as providing more attractive power for industrial purposes. There is no probability about it: the payment of subventions will definitely assist the coal industry and this is of vital importance to us in my area because the coal industry is our bread and butter.
It was mentioned by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond that our proposition had improved a wee bit since the proposal of his government was made on March 14. That "wee bit of improvement" in which we are so interested amounts, I believe, to approximately $1,700,000 yearly in subventions. The minister could correct me if I am wrong in that figure. To my knowledge no mention was ever made to the payment of subventions until the proposal of the present government was outlined, as verified by the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond also said that it did not become an election issue. It certainly was an election issue in my area because we were vitally interested in this question which was extremely important to us.
There is a tremendous difference, with a capital "D", in the pre-election plan offered at the last minute by the previous government, and the one we have before us today. This plan has been hailed, welcomed and acclaimed by provincial leaders, civic leaders and by newspapers, not only in the Atlantic provinces but throughout Canada, and also by the coal miners who are the group most vitally concerned and by the leaders of the miners' union and others. I do not have as much time as some other hon. members and my scissors are not very sharp so I did not have an opportunity to clip all the newspaper articles and editorial comment expressing support of this measure but many comments have appeared in the press since this announcement was made. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond read several press comments into the record and I could do the same thing. One article to which I have already referred is entitled, "Muscle for the Maritimes" and reads:
The Conservative government is being true, not only to its election promises, but to its whole concept of national development, when it announces large-scale measures to promote production and distribution of cheap power in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

Would my hon. friend tell me from what newspaper he is quoting.



Atlantic Provinces Power Development Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
That is to be found in the Cape Breton Post a good paper and it is quoted from the Toronto Globe and Mail. I have another editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of November 16, 1957.
Oh, oh.

speechtext: You know, I am one of those of whom a so-called great Liberal leader said they should be put in padded cells. I am a coal miner and that comment was made by a so-called great leader of the Liberal party.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: If the plan of the previous administration was as good as the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond stated it was when a gentleman named Mr. Harris announced it, why did the people of Nova Scotia show their resentment toward the plan by returning ten Conservative members out of a possible 12 from Nova Scotia.
You explained that yourself by telling us about the Conservative promises made before the election.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I should like to quote what Mr. John H. Delaney, international board member of the United mine workers of district 26, had to say shortly after the announcement:
We very much welcome the announcement by the federal government that thermal power plants will be erected in the maritimes. The plan is an excellent thing for Nova Scotia's coal industry. Anything that will expand the maritime market for coal is good for the industry. The government's plan as announced last week will not only provide cheap power for industry, but will very materially help the coal industry.
That is a very important point-helping the coal industry.

There has been some controversy within the last day or so as to what the Leader of the Opposition said at some meeting in Fredericton. I was quite interested. I had not followed it before; it had not appeared in our local papers, but I made it my business to look it up and I have it here as it appeared in the Daily Gleaner of Fredericton for May 24, 1957. I should like to take this opportunity to say that what the hon. member for Cape Breton South said yesterday was quite right. Absolutely right. I should like to quote part of the article. An editorial appeared in the paper some time previous to the meeting and it was in relation to that editorial that the Leader of the Opposition made his remarks at the meeting, and I should like to quote from the article:
After quoting the editorial, Mr. St. Laurent would not venture to say how much power would cost in New Brunswick. It was an engineering proposition that would have to be investigated. If it was found that power could not be produced at reasonable prices the Atlantic provinces would have to do without it.
However, the Prime Minister expressed confidence that power could be produced at "reasonable and competitive prices".
I am covering the article pretty well; I am not just picking out certain parts. I continue:
Purpose of the federal offer to construct thermal plants was to bring cheaper power to the maritimes; not primarily to aid coal mines in Nova Scotia.
Remember he said "not primarily" to aid coal mines in Nova Scotia.
Mr. St. Laurent believed that eventually-
This is the point that the hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned yesterday:
-coal would be too valuable a material for production of synthetic products to be used as a fuel. He did not want to see coal centres turned into "ghost towns", but he would not encourage any immediate substantial increase in coal production.
It would not be fair to future generations in the maritimes who would greatly benefit from the increased value of coal as an industrial raw material. If federal-developed thermal power aided Nova Scotia coal mines, that was "incidental and will be all for the good".
That is what the former prime minister said.
Incidental! That is more or less Liberal thinking, incidental as far as the maritimes are concerned.
Let us get back to the resolution. I should like to make a very important observation. Let me say that we have come a long way when we look back and recall the visit of the former minister of fisheries in the previous government to the maritimes. This has been mentioned in the house on another occasion, but I should like to refresh the memories of my friends opposite. At that time the hon. member for Coast-Capilano opened his mouth and put his foot in it with

his infamous statement that uneconomical coal mines must eventually close. Close them up! It does not make any difference. Close them all up, nothing can be done about them!
Don't even consider if anything can be done. It was a simple matter for the hon. member to make this rash statement, but it is not so simple for a miner to leave his home and everything he has accumulated through years of hard, dirty, miserable and dangerous work. And this is what he would have to do because we do not have any other industry to which he can turn. It is no wonder that the union officials of Princess local union of the united mineworkers of America at Sydney Mines, my home town, termed this statement brazen and a black eye to organized workers in the coal industry in my province. I can think of other words that may have been used. What a contrast, Mr. Chairman, what a picture! We have on the one hand a member of the Liberal government coming into our own back yard and with unmitigated gall kicking us in the teeth. This is a do-nothing-for-you, a take-you-no-where and a kick-you-after-he-gets-you-there policy.
As far as the maritimes are concerned, this has been the policy of the Liberal party in the past; it is their present policy and it shall continue to be their policy in the future. On the other hand, we have a government which is composed of men who are dedicated to the job of providing good legislation, and they have proven it in the short time that they have been in office, not only for the maritimes but for all of Canada.
When I began my remarks I mentioned that I was proud that this legislation had been introduced by a Conservative government. Let me reiterate that once more. I have to interrupt myself because I have something here that is very important, namely another statement from the office of the united mineworkers of America at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia. This local represents roughly 10,000 men at the moment. I should like to quote the following paragraph:
It will take some time for the government program to be completed, but "we hope the proposal to pay subventions on coal used in power production will apply right away".
That is the thing we are interested in and that is the thing we were interested in during the campaign. Let me reiterate once more that I am doubly proud that we have as our leader the Prime Minister, a great man who will not only be noted in history as the man of the year 1957, but the man of the century in Canada.
Atlantic Provinces Power Development

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this resolution. Let me say at the outset, as some other members from the west have already said, that I am indeed pleased to know that New Brunswick is getting some assistance. It does not matter to me particularly what government they get it from so long as they get it. The Atlantic provinces are one part of Canada which has not received the same consideration that other parts of Canada have received, neither have the western provinces received the same assistance as have other parts of Canada. Therefore I am grateful that on this occasion at least the Atlantic provinces are getting some consideration.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, the time has long passed when we should have legislation in this country which discriminates against one part of the community as compared with another. Over the last few years we have had several examples of that discrimination. One example that comes to my mind is the freight rate structure of Canada. The Atlantic provinces and the western provinces have been discriminated against in the matter of freight rates ever since confederation. It is no wonder that some of the provinces are complaining bitterly at the present time about that discrimination and are asking that some assistance be given them in this respect.
As I say, I am glad to know that the Atlantic provinces are getting assistance. I do not want anything that I might say to be construed in any way as being opposed to assistance to the Atlantic provinces. In fact, Mr. Chairman, on many occasions in this house I have emphasized the importance and the necessity of giving assistance to the Atlantic provinces so that they might be brought on a par with the central provinces of Canada. I have also urged that the western provinces might be brought on a par with the central provinces because, in my opinion, it is not good economically, it is not good nationally that the two central provinces should be given assistance that will be of greater benefit to them than to the other parts of Canada.
I said a moment ago that I thought the .freight rate structure of this country was discriminatory against the Atlantic provinces and the western provinces, and I want to say that this bill is discriminatory also in its effect. I think, in that sense, it is bad. Certainly I know the Atlantic provinces need assistance in generating electrical power. I happened to be there a couple of years ago and I can say without hesitation that, in my judgment at least, the Atlantic provinces are

Atlantic Provinces Power Development 10 to 15 years behind the central provinces because ol the discrimination which has existed in the past. We in the west are fighting to the utmost extent of our ability in trying to make some progress against the obstacles which have been placed in our way by the central provinces.
Here we have a resolution which, in my judgment, is discriminatory against every part of Canada. I am not referring to the central provinces when I say that. The resolution before us, according to the minister, has two main purposes in mind. He says this, as reported at page 3037 of Hansard for January 8, 1958:
As announced in this house on November 14, 1957, by the Prime Minister, apart from the financing of Beechwood, which is being dealt with separately, the present proposed measure would do two things. For those Atlantic provinces who desire such aid the dominion government would build for and sell to the provinces such thermal plants and transmission facilities as may be agreed upon. The second part of the program would consist of granting a subvention on Atlantic provinces' coal consumed for the production of power in the Atlantic provinces. This subvention would be so calculated as to eliminate, so far as possible, the differential in price between coal used in the Atlantic area and coal used in Ontario for the production of power.
Thus not only is assistance to be given in this way, but he said that in the future there would undoubtedly be other programs submitted which would require to be considered by parliament. This is, therefore, a rather extensive program. We hope that the results of the resolution will be beneficial to the Atlantic provinces. We hope also that this element of discrimination is removed. It is quite obvious because the resolution itself says:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with any of the Atlantic provinces to provide assistance in the generation of electric energy by thermal electric power projects and in the control and transmission of electric energy,-
This is important.
-and including provisions for the payment of a subvention on coal used in the production of electric energy.
Why does the government confine it to the Atlantic provinces? Why not say that the government will enter into agreements with any province to provide the same facilities as they are providing under this measure for the Atlantic provinces? I thought this Conservative government was going to do something about the development of Canada, but here we have a measure which, in its effect, is going to carry out the same policy of discrimination as was carried out by the other government. I was in hopes that this government would do something on a national

basis to help all those have-not provinces, instead of confirming this measure of aid to one section of the country.
I want to speak about this subvention on coal. We, in the province of Alberta, produce electric power by two means, by hydro and by this thermal process. It is difficult for some of the thermal units to compete with hydro. I believe that in the city of Edmonton they have switched to gas. They had no assistance when they were forced to use coal. Then, down in the Drumheller area we produce electric power from coal. We have had no assistance.
Now, substantial assistance is going to be given to the coal mining industry of New Brunswick and the other Atlantic provinces. I am glad to see them get it, because in the last few years they have been in very great difficulty. We in Alberta have been in the same position, so why discriminate against Alberta? I am not going to speak about coal at this time, but I did put these figures on Hansard just the other day, and I want to say that over the last four or five years the Alberta mines have been forced to close at the rate of 15 to 20 mines a year. Our production is continually falling.
The last speaker was referring to some of the promises made by the Prime Minister in the Atlantic areas, which he is now carrying out. What about the promises he made concerning the production of coal in our provinces? A number of mines closed again in the first eight months of last year, and production went down considerably.
Why not change governments?
God forbid that anything like that would happen.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Don't be so serious.

This is a serious problem. I am amazed at the attitude of the hon. member when he asks, why don't we change governments. Surely he recognizes that there is discrimination in this legislation. He should be the first one in this house to object to this type of legislation. Let him come out in the province of Alberta and he will see that the only reason we have been progressing is that we have not had either a Liberal or Conservative government.
What about oil?
Oil has done a lot, but what have you fellows down here done to our oil industry? You have practically ruined the oil industry because of your trade policies with the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

These are the tactics used by this so-called progressive government; the Diefenbaker government.
Let us examine the extent to which this project is going to assist the coal mining industry of the Atlantic provinces. It is going to be a very substantial amount. Let me say that I am glad they are getting that assistance.
Then why do you object?
Because of the unfair treatment that is given to the west in regard to coal.
Why not do that another year?

Let us not wait for another bill. All you have to do is leave out that word "Atlantic" and put in the word "any". My friends might think this is a joke, but I am afraid that when it comes time for another election they will not see the joke. All we are trying to do now is make sure this thing will not be used as a political football.
