I am just answering some of their questions, Mr. Chairman. I might add that they did their best to kill that measure entirely. But of course I do not intend to speak about the pipe line at this time. I want to refer to another part of the minister's remarks in this regard. At page 3039 of Hansard he states this about the subvention:
The rate of assistance per ton will vary with the quality of the coal used in the individual plants. For example, a plant using coal with a heat value of 13,325 B.T.U. per pound would qualify for $1.81 per ton at the rate of 6.78 cents per million B.T.U., while another plant using coal of 11,190 B.T.U. per pound would rate $1.62.
Just before that, as reported at page 3038 of Hansard, he points out:
The second phase of the government's program will consist of a subvention on the Atlantic provinces' coal used for the production of thermal electric energy in the Atlantic provinces. For the purpose of this resolution the annual cost of such a subvention is currently estimated to amount to $1.7 million.
I wonder whether the members of the Conservative party have given a thought to what amount of assistance that sum of money would give in restoring our coal industry in western Canada. We also could use this subvention on coal for the production of electric power. When we are talking about these subventions for this particular purpose, let us make the measure apply to all parts of Canada. Then if there were other parts of Canada that do not want to use it, that would be their affair. The measure would be there for them to use if they desire to do so. Then it cannot be said that it is cheaper to produce your power by hydro or that it is cheaper to use natural gas. If that is the case, then of course none of those provinces would apply for assistance and there should be then no objection to removing this restriction.
We in the province of Alberta are in a mighty bad position so far as our coal industry is concerned and such assistance as this, if it were applied to other parts of Canada, would be of great help. We have hundreds and hundreds of coal miners who are out of work, just as you had in the Atlantic provinces. You were seeking a way in which to be able to re-open some of these

Atlantic Provinces Power Development mines, to assist the mines and the people so employed, and you figure that this is one way in which to do it. I am sure that it will. But why deprive those of us in the rest of Canada from getting that same assistance? We have many miners out there in my constituency alone who are out of a job now and who have exhausted their unemployment insurance. There is no place else for them to go because they are coal miners. Yet we do not get any assistance like this.
Surely it is time that the government of Canada began to enact legislation which would be of equal benefit all over the country so that all parts of Canada would be able to expand industrially thus giving them the same standard of living as is enjoyed by the two central provinces. When you do anything that counteracts that high principle then I think you are on the wrong road and you should change the legislation or amend it so that things will be equal, wherever it is possible to do so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The attitude of some of the hon. members opposite in the debate is most amazing to me. First of all, I think that reference should be made to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and his amazing position during these last two days. He is the only former Liberal cabinet minister from the Atlantic provinces left after the debacle in the last election. He is also, I understand, the Liberal caucus chairman of the members of that party from the Atlantic provinces, and I would think he would be obliged to speak up for any measures that would benefit one of those provinces. Yet we see the example here today and yesterday of an attack on this legislation that would definitely benefit one of those provinces in which he is supposed to be interested.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair. As to the Beechwood matter which is not under debate now, I said that I would not oppose something that was good for New Brunswick merely because the government would not tell us how the principle would apply in other provinces. But I think I had a perfect right to inquire how it would apply in the province I represent. When I spoke about this measure today I said it was an excellent resolution, and I have nothing to take back.
[Mr. Johnston (Bow River).)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I certainly
would think that a man with the hon. member's 20 years of experience in parliament could use the term "excellent" without taking two days to do it. However, the stand of some of the other members from the maritimes- and I am referring to them in this instance- is also amazing. The hon. member for Charlotte who has always opposed this Beechwood project-
He did not speak in this debate.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I was severely restricted by Your Honour and other members from the chair yesterday in debating Beechwood. Surely you are not going to permit the hon. member to debate Beechwood on another resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

During the course of the
minister's answer a few minutes ago he pointed to the fact that the agreement he is about to reach with the provinces is much more advantageous for the autonomy of the provinces than the proposal that had been advanced by the previous administration in that the present government would build the plants and transmission lines and, as he said yesterday, the provinces would have to purchase them immediately at cost and pay for them over a period of years. I might remind the minister that Mr. Harris, when he made the offer of the previous government in his budget speech of March 14 last, offered Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the opportunity of purchasing the plants and transmission lines at any time they wished. I quote from page 2220 of Hansard of March 14, 1957:
Under this proposal, the transmission lines would be rented on a non-profit basis and the power would be sold at cost to provincial electric systems. The purpose would be that the plants and other

facilities built under this program can be acquired by the provinces at any time on payment of their amortized cost.
The minister should not forget that when the present administration took over we were negotiating with the two provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and that no final agreement had been reached. He will agree that some principles had been put forward, principles which have been kept and rightly so by the present administration in the agreements they are trying to reach with the two provinces now and which are the object of this resolution. If the minister looks at the file-I have here Sessional Paper No. 117 tabled on Friday, January 3, 1958-he will see that correspondence was maintained between the premiers of the two provinces and myself until the end of April. Then, of course, I was rather busy for some time and the deputy minister of the department continued the correspondence, while the officials, according to this sessional paper, carried on negotiations at the official level on technical matters.
At that time, as will be recalled, we were waiting for the report of the Montreal Engineering Company, which was absolutely necessary before we could reach a final agreement with the two provinces concerned. This program, therefore, was initiated in March by the previous administration, was discussed and was evolved until there was a change of government on June 21.
On July 12, according to this correspondence, the premier of New Brunswick wrote to the then minister of northern affairs, now Minister of Agriculture, and the negotiations were continued up to the time that agreement could be reached. Agreement has been reached on certain principles but there are still some matters to be settled before agreements can be signed. I do not see how this present government could contend that the previous government had not done whatever was possible to try to reach agreement with the provinces, respecting their autonomy, in consultation with those two provinces; and what the government has done is just to continue the negotiations that had been started previously on the principles which were enunciated both by Mr. Harris and myself last spring.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Including
Beechwood.

Beechwood has nothing to do with this resolution. I discussed Beechwood yesterday and I made the position of the previous government very clear on Beechwood. This resolution deals with a program *for thermal installations and transmission 96698-196i
Atlantic Provinces Power Development lines in the Atlantic provinces. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I think we have to clear this matter up once and for all. I know that it has been ruled that I cannot speak on anything else but this thermal plant measure, but the whole thing would not have been even possible without getting the cost down. We could not get the cost down if we did not combine thermal and hydro. That was why I said "including Beechwood". The hon. member rode over that question and implied that this program we have announced is the same as that of the previous government. But I can say quite frankly that it is not so on that point, and that we could not have met this test without tying in with hydro.

I agree first that the test that we had in mind, as expressed in my intervention on April 9, on the subvention on coal is not the same as the one that is being proposed in this resolution. With that I agree. I agree that we were not ready at the time to make a loan on Beechwood; but I do not agree that that program was not to have an interconnection between Beechwood and the thermal plants. Of course it was the program, and the minister knows it very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: The point I am trying to get through the member's head is that the cost of hydro power depends on the interest rate and that one fact does not seem to have sunk in here. If we are going to get the cost down on these thermal plants we have to get the cost down on the hydro. One of the members asked a question the other day along that line. I do not like to raise my voice in this connection,-
Do not do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext: Surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Therefore the saving will be greater and we are helping the province much more if we use a load factor that is higher. In giving this figure today at an 85 per cent load factor I was giving the government's maximum position in helping the province.
The first thing you know you are going to get me into this thing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I take this opportunity to congratulate both hon. members for their endeavour to keep their remarks within the confines of the resolution which is before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I think that at the moment I was trying to make a correction.

May I at this point say a word as to what the minister replied to me regarding the cost of power at Beechwood, his answer to the question from the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond was that the cost of Beechwood power with an interest rate of 6 per cent, was between 7 and 7.5 mills. The load factor was not mentioned. But because the figure of 300 million kilowatt hours utilization was mentioned I felt it was an 85 per cent load factor that was used to come to that conclusion. But the minister in his answer a few moments ago told the committee that the cost in mills on a 50 per cent load factor was 7.3 mills for the two units at Beechwood, did he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: No.
They are both wrong. It is not the load factor which governs: it is the power factor.
Would the minister look at the sheet he read slowly: 72 megawatts; money at 6 per cent; load factor, 50 per cent; cost 7.3 mills.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: That is right.

That is what the minister read into the record. So how do we reconcile this explanation with the one he
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

gave to the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. If the minister would rather reply on second reading, I do not mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I am not questioning this. The whole thing, Mr. Chairman, to my mind, makes it impossible for me, with the two sets of figures I have here, to come up with an answer that is to the point because on top of the detail that I have I must have time to work out these answers. I wish the whole matter had been left to the committee stage where I could have dealt with it with some help.

May I, in all seriousness, make a suggestion at this point of the resolution stage. May I suggest that those who want to discuss the matter-and I speak now as an electrician since 1924-of peak load, power load or power factor, which is entirely different, adjourn to the coffee shop with the rest of us and discuss the principle of the resolution that is now before us.

When the minister began his reply a short time ago he said that this legislation was designed to meet a specific problem. That specific problem must be the shortage of electric power. That, I take it, is what the problem is.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: High rates.
I beg the minister's pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I am just being very peaceful in my suggestion. The problem was that they could not bring industry into the area because the rates for industrial power were too high. So we went in in order to try to help them bring them down so that they could attract industry which would cause a greater demand for power and then your demand would start to rise.
Are you saying that there is no shortage of power and that the only purpose is to create more power in order to bring down or lower the rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: What I am saying is that there was a need for low cost or cheap power in the maritimes.
And more power. Is that not right?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Yes; because if you are going to produce cheap power, you are going to need more in order to meet the demand.

Yes. We have the same specific problem in Newfoundland. There is in my own riding a * fluorspar mine closed down at this moment because one of the factors in the cost of their production is the cost of*

electricity. In my riding there is also a fish processing plant which is closed down at the present time because they cannot operate with a sufficiently low cost and one of the factors in their cost of production is the shortage of electricity in addition to the high cost of electricity. Both these factors are present.
How, then, does the government propose to meet that problem in Newfoundland under this legislation? The minister when speaking a little while ago mentioned the development of water power being assigned to Brinco, the British Newfoundland Corporation. That is only partially true. There are many sources of hydro power on a smaller scale which do not come under the jurisdiction of Brinco. Brinco is concerned with the huge development on Hamilton falls in Labrador and also with the watershed development in the Bay d'Espoir area, which has a possibility of producing 500 thousand horsepower.
There are, however, many other sources of hydroelectric power on a smaller scale but which do not come under Brinco at all and which are necessary for the development of Newfoundland island-particularly for the development in my own riding which is a "have-not" riding. Furthermore its only chance of survival is the utilization of the power resources which we have, and that is why we are so anxious to have this resolution made applicable to Newfoundland.
We are happy in what is being done for the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and we are supporting this legislation, but we have a similar problem and would like to see something done under this legislation particularly in view of the fact that it is part of a national plan. If it were only a special project for those two provinces and not part of a national plan then I do not think we would have a very strong case, but as part of a national plan and in view of our need surely we have some claim for consideration under this legislation.
I could not follow the minister very well in his reference to Newfoundland. He spoke of hoping that some day something would be done; that Newfoundland would on some way avail herself of the benefits under this legislation. He spoke of transmission lines but I could not really follow his thoughts when he was speaking and I do wish he would be more specific. I ask him now to tell us in more detail just what he envisages for Newfoundland in this legislation. Transmission lines are not distributing lines. If you are going to transmit something you must have something to transmit. It must be developed somewhere. Are you going to develop it in the maritimes by using coal? We
Atlantic Provinces Power Development could develop it much more cheaply in Newfoundland by using hydro power.
If we are going to use coal then we would have to pay a subvention on the coal, we would have to pay freight to get it over to Newfoundland and all the handling charges between the areas, which would double the price. The price of coal in Newfoundland is just about double what it is in North Sydney and if you are going to use North Sydney coal to run the thermal plants in Newfoundland the cost is going to be terrific. Why should a federal government tie its hands in this manner and bind itself to excessive costs when the same thing could be done much more cheaply and exactly the same problem could be met in a much better way by the development of electric power?
I would be most grateful to the minister if he would tell me exactly how this legislation is going to benefit Newfoundland.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister replies to my colleague from Burin-Burgeo I should like to join him in his plea and I also want to make one or two other observations. I should like at once to reassure you, Mr. Chairman, that I do not intend to go beyond the ground covered by the minister himself, and I assume that it will be permissible for me to touch upon any subject touched upon by the minister without my being called to order.
I tried without any kind of success to find out certain things from the Minister of Finance yesterday and I must say I congratulate the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources on his attitude to the committee. Unlike the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is conciliatory and friendly and does try his best to give us what information he has. What I fear is that he is very seriously limited by the uncertainty in the government of which he is a member about what their policy is. I am afraid that is not his disability but it is the disability of the government.
I could not agree more completely with the excellent analysis of the situation in Newfoundland as given by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. It is true of course that the Hamilton river, with the Columbia river is, I suppose, the greatest undeveloped source of hydroelectric power in the western world, if not in the whole world. It is also true that it is in the province of Newfoundland but it is in that part of the province which is on the mainland of Canada, and a good deal of time is going to pass before very much of the power from the Hamilton river becomes available on the island of Newfoundland.

Atlantic Provinces Power Development
It is also true, as the hon. member said, that there are one or two large undeveloped sites in Newfoundland which are at the present time under the control of the British Newfoundland Corporation, but there are around the shores of Newfoundland some 1300 settlements in which a series of small sites could be developed, in most cases at no terribly great cost and which no doubt could be self-sufficient if they could be developed cheaply enough. But, as the minister so accurately said when he referred to his own province of Saskatchewan, one difficulty has been the rate of interest which either a private company or the government of Newfoundland would have had to pay for financing these developments. Another difficulty is the one which small projects of this sort have in getting organized and developing on an individual scale. That is, I happen to know, what prompted the premier of Newfoundland to make the request to the Prime Minister shortly after this motion was put on the order paper that its scope should be enlarged to include the development of hydro plants.
The premier did not have in mind, and I know this because I have discussed it with him, large developments like that on the Hamilton river. He had in mind the relatively small developments with which the minister will be familiar and which serve what I suppose we must call the rural communities of Newfoundland although the word rural has an agricultural connotation which is perhaps not entirely accurate. There is no part of Canada where this power development is more needed than Newfoundland in order to give anything like equality of opportunity or anything like a comparable standard of living-not even New Brunswick.
It seems to me that the government could have made this excellent measure very much better by accepting our suggestion. It is not as though they had not been asked to do it; they were asked to do it some time ago by the premier of Newfoundland. All he asked them to do was bring hydro development within the ambit of their legislation. It seems to me that was a most eminently reasonable suggestion, and it would not have committed the government to supporting any scheme which was not reasonable or proper; it would simply have made it possible for Newfoundland to have been included in this national policy about which the government boasted in the speech from the throne.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Does he agree with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that hydroelectric

development in Newfoundland would be much cheaper than thermal development-and that would apply either to Nova Scotia or to New Brunswick-and would not the cost of the transmission lines be the place where Newfoundland would be benefitted. Is not that where this resolution and the bill which will be brought in is intended to assist Newfoundland to equalize the cost of power in that province with that of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick? The hon. member has just repeated-

The hon. member was
asking a question, not making a speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Does he agree then with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that hydro development in Newfoundland would be much cheaper than thermal development, either in Newfoundland, New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, and if it is his argument does not apply.
I am very grateful to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who has an extraordinary faculty of reminding us of good points for our arguments that we sometimes forget.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I have listened to so many bad arguments that-
He is, in a way which is quite characteristic of the government to which he belongs, offering another Indian gift.
You can talk about Indians.
I listened politely to the hon. gentleman when he was interrupting me and perhaps he would not mind listening to me now.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Well, answer my question.

I am, and very directly.
I am saying that transmission lines at the present time to connect the various power stations in Newfoundland would be of little or no value because of the great distances between the various units in that province. What is needed in that province is, as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo so accurately, said, the development of new small plants to overcome the difficulties caused by these long distances.
Unlike the hon. member for Vancouver East, I have no expertise in these matters, and do not pretend to have any. It is no doubt true that it is cheaper to develop hydro power, though that would depend a good deal on the site and on the situation, but I would remind the Minister of Veterans Affairs that if you have not the money to do anything at all, it is no easier to buy hamburger than it is to buy a first class steak,

and we in Newfoundland see no reason why we should be allowed to have hamburger when in the hon. gentleman's province they have filet mignon.

This is a baloney
sandwich.

That is all I am urging. I am urging the government once again, and urging the minister, to do something along the lines we are suggesting, because I believe the minister has a good deal more sympathy with our proposals than has the Minister of Finance, and perhaps that is understandable. I suspect that one reason why he should be sympathetic is that the hon. gentleman hopes to come to this house some day before a certain event happens, and ask us to vote considerable sums of money for a power development which was supposed to have started 30 days ago in his own province. He is going to find it more difficult than ever, when he comes to do that to justify his refusal, and the refusal of the government, to include the very modest demands which the hon. members for Burin-Burgeo, Humber-St. George's, Trinity-Conception and I are making to have the facilities provided under this resolution made available to Newfoundland.
Now the minister also said that we must take it on trust when the Prime Minister said that any scheme for which an equally good case could be made out would be considered on its merits, that any scheme for which an equally good case could be made out would come within the scope of the principles of the national development policy embodied in Beechwood.
It may be that it would be quite unnecessary to include hydro development in Newfoundland within the scope of this measure if the minister could give us an unqualified assurance that a loan at the rate of interest and on the same terms as Beechwood would be available for any reasonable project in the province of Newfoundland or in any other province. If the minister could give us an unqualified assurance to that effect, if he could outline precisely what the national policy is, we on this side would be far more satisfied than we are at present.
All we know, and all he has told us on the subject, is that that national scheme consists of two projects in New Brunswick and one in Nova Scotia, a project in Saskatchewan and a project in British Columbia-four provinces out of ten. Every one of these projects was well known before the present government took office. There has been no suggestion yet of anything new in this entire national policy. Our suggestion is that the
Atlantic Provinces Power Development national policy should be extended to the province of Newfoundland. The hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that it should be extended to the minister's own province; one or two hon. members from Alberta suggested its extension there, and the hon. member for New Westminster suggested its extension to British Columbia-

And
the member for Winnipeg North Centre will be on his feet in a minute.

I was just going to say, when the hon. member interrupted me, that I feel there is an obligation upon me to say a word on behalf of my hon. friend, the hon. -member for St. Boniface, who is not here today because he has to be at home because of the illness of his wife. I know that he also wishes to make an appeal on behalf of his province. The minister knows that the premier of Manitoba, in the course of the federal-provincial conference-I know the minister is aware of this because he was there at the time-made during the presentation of his brief a formal request to be included.
As nearly as I have been able to gather from the minister's remarks, and from everything that has been said, the government has no ideas of its own; it is waiting for requests from the provinces. Now they have had a formal request from the premier of Newfoundland which they have not been willing to accept up to now.
I am trying to make my language as moderate as possible in the hope of melting the minister's heart and in the hope that perhaps he will be able to persuade his colleagues to do the decent thing by Newfoundland. He may even get some assistance from my broadminded colleague on the other side of the house from Saint John-Albert. I hope that when the hon. gentleman is elevated to the cabinet with the other young men who are soon to take the place, we were told yesterday, or was it this morning, of the present incumbents of treasury benches, we from Newfoundland will get a little consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I ever do get into the cabinet I am not sneaking in through the back door.

The hon. gentleman can compare his majority and his proportion of the vote with mine, and if he would like to come and contest my riding against me he is very welcome; I would not be at all worried. I may say, sir, and I say it with pride that there is no member in this house who has a greater right to speak here on behalf of his constituents, except my hon.
3098	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development friend from Burin-Burgeo who was acclaimed. There is no other member of this house who has a greater right to claim he represents his constituents, because 87 out of every 100 who voted, voted for me, and when the hon. member for Saint John-Albert has the same kind of majority from his constituency he can talk about people getting into this house through the back door.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I did not say that the hon. member came into this House of Commons by the back door; I said he entered the cabinet by what is considered by many people to be the back door.

Mr. Chairman, I think
everyone knows that I had a position in the civil service which I am inclined to think, if the words of the present Minister of Public Works mean anything, would have been secure even after June 10 and it does not seem to me that anyone who suggests that to give up that kind of position to accept what do seem to be the hazards of public life and who I think most hon. members will admit has accepted them rather cheerfully, accurately describes the situation in referring to my entry into the cabinet as being by the back door.
The hon. member should sell tickets for this show.
I think perhaps that on reflection the hon. member would agree that he is not correct in suggesting that that is entering by the back door.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Sit down.
Perhaps if and when the hon. gentleman arrives in the cabinet he will have to crawl in the coal hole.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I will at least run in my own riding. I will not have to go out in the middle of the Atlantic ocean to get elected.

I hasten to withdraw that remark, Mr. Chairman, because I have the highest regard for the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public Works and I know he would grace any position in the cabinet. As a matter of fact I can think of one or two members of the cabinet for whom I would cheerfully substitute him.
However, sir, I must confess that I think, myself, I am getting a little out of order, and I should like to return to my very serious plea. It does seem to me that it is time we were told what this national policy for power development really is, what it comprises, how a province qualifies, how a project qualifies, what the criteria are. It also seems to me that


if the minister had brought down real enabling legislation it would have laid down the qualification for all projects in all parts of Canada.
You played that record for us last night, why not change it?
Oh, I would change it very quickly if the hon. gentleman is impatient about it.
If you must sing, why not put a little more music into it?

It would be very easy for the government to silence me and to do so with my consent, if the government would answer these perfectly proper questions that are being put to it, if it would reveal what its national policy is, how it applies in the province I represent and how it applies in the other five provinces about which we have been told nothing until now.
I think this is an excellent measure. It was devised by the Liberal government and accepted by two Tory provincial governments before the election and all we have had since are some minor modifications. It is still a good measure and I am certainly going to support it, but I am doing my best to encourage the government to make it a better measure. I am also doing my best to get from the government some indication of how this policy applies across the country. I want to know how it applies to Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Newfoundland and the other provinces. How do the provinces qualify? What projects qualify? What is an "equally good case"? What are the merits? Surely we are not being asked to accept this blindly.
I conclude by appealing again to the minister to adjourn this debate, to meet with his colleagues and see if he cannot persuade them to get a royal message so that this resolution could be slightly modified to carry out what we have been asking for all day.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If this is a policy of the former Liberal government how did you propose to make it apply to all of Canada? You have repeatedly said it was your policy.

What I said, Mr. Chairman, was that the projects that are embodied in this resolution were proposed by Mr. Harris in his budget debate and amplified by my colleague, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet. I did not say that the previous administration had a national policy for power development and I never pretended it did because it did not. We never pretended we had. The difference is that hon. gentlemen opposite boasted about it, put the words in Her Majesty's mouth and now when we ask what those words mean we are told we have not the right to know, it is something that

Atlantic Provinces Power Development
will be revealed in due course. That is the favourite phrase of this government. Members of the government used to complain about the previous administration referring to the public interest. The expression of this government is, "You children on the other side will be told in due course if you are good boys. Do not talk too much. Do not ask too many questions".
Hear, hear.

The government says, "Just listen to John, let him do all the talking; and then in his own good time, if he feels inclined, he may tell you a little about what these empty phrases"-and I am afraid that is all they are

"really mean."
That is all we got from the Liberal government for 22 years, talk and no action. Now you are getting action.
What about the St. Lawrence seaway?

We are getting action on
that, too.

Mr. Chairman, with the exception of intervals of a few minutes on various occasions I have been here and have listened with keen interest to the entire debate on this resolution today. I hope that through you, sir, I can tell this government and future governments that perhaps we can learn a lesson from this debate. The government has introduced a measure which is without doubt of major importance. It embodies the principle of providing assistance to the Atlantic provinces in certain phases of power development and the transmission of power. Because of the way it is framed it has of necessity given rise to the question in the minds of hon. members from other parts of Canada as to whether or not the same principle will be applied in other provinces if requests are made by the governments of the provinces irrespective of their party affiliations. That is an important question which I believe all have the right to ask.
I did not rise at this time to bring up the question of British Columbia, Saskatchewan or Newfoundland and indeed I have been trying for quite a while to figure out a way to explain the point I wish to raise. I feel that consideration should be given in the future, and perhaps it ought to be given at this time, to referring this question to a committee for study because if you have followed all the discussion today, as I am certain you have, Mr. Chairman, you will be aware that a great deal of confusion and
complexity has arisen concerning the meaning of the principle of the resolution and the engineering aspects of the project envisaged by the resolution.
We have heard from the minister, and almost everyone who has spoken, questions on engineering aspects which underly the principle of this bill, and they were introduced by the minister himself.
I ask you quite honestly, sir, how many of us sitting here as members of the House of Commons can pass on a bill when a great deal of it is bound up in engineering facets and factors? How many of us are in a position to make a decision, especially when watts are thrown around? Watts of what? What is a kilowatt? What is a k.v.a.? What is horsepower? What is the term that has been used so often, which actually means one million watts? We have had such terms as peak load and power load but no reference to the most important of all from an engineering point of view, namely electrical or power factor. Let us not kid ourselves, the power factor could mean a lot more than a peak load or a power load, especially in electrical engineering.
Therefore, sir, I hope you understand the point I am trying to make. Here we have a resolution, the principle of which I think we all agree with. How far it goes we are not sure and we are trying to find out. Some of the major arguments which have been put forward by the minister who introduced the resolution were on the basis of electrical engineering facts and terminology which most of us do not understand. Perhaps a few of us do understand them.
The minister read from a script and I as an electrician can tell him that he was wrong in some of the terms he used. What he is after is a grid system in New Brunswick and in Nova Scotia, which I hope will eventually be extended all across Canada, but a grid system was not mentioned. My hon. friend from Newfoundland-I can never remember his constituency-
Bonavista-Twillingate.
I cannot learn French because there are some English names I cannot remember.
It was the beginning of everything in Canada.

The hon. member discussed Newfoundland. Of course, he is interested in Newfoundland and in its development but he does not know a darn thing about electrical engineering and electronics. I could tell that from his speech.

I admit it.

Supply-Justice

In electricity today is not yesterday. Today not only are we changing from copper to aluminum above ground but the same thing applies to undersea cables. In the past they were 77,000 volts and 220,000 volts but now they are 750,000 volts and this has changed the complete idea of the distribution of electricity. Therefore it might be better to produce electricity 750 miles away and distribute it. These are matters of engineering, electronics and electricity which have been thrown into the debate. I say, sir, although it happens to be my trade, I am not in a position to debate it either. I hope that as long as this debate continues we shall keep to the principle of the bill which indicates that the federal government is now going to take some action on a public basis to assist the expansion of power in two provinces. We hope we shall get an answer that it will apply to any other province which makes a request for assistance.
If we cannot do so with respect to this bill, I hope that in the future when a minister presents an argument that is based on his reading of engineering reports, the bill, after it passes the resolution stage, will be referred to a responsible and respected committee of the House of Commons before which engineers can be called to explain exactly what it means. I am certain that if that procedure had been followed in this resolution we would not have taken as long on it as we have done.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 244, to provide assistance in respect of electric power development in the Atlantic provinces.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock. Mr. Winch: Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting for a number of months for an opportunity of asking the Minister of Justice 
his views and policies on certain matters. I had intended to discuss the matter of capital and corporal punishment under the minister's estimates, but in view of the fact I have a bill for the abolition of capital punishment up for second reading, and have given notice of a bill for the abolition of corporal punishment, I believe that according to parliamentary procedure I should not discuss these two subjects. It is not my intention this evening, therefore, to go into the matter of capital or corporal punishment because, as I have said, of the two bills I have, one on the order paper and the other of which I have given notice.
There are matters which come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice which are of the utmost importance and upon which I think, in this first session of a new parliament, an opportunity should be given to the minister to explain the government's policy. I believe we should, therefore, ask for a statement from him at this time.
First of all, sir, I should like to draw to your attention the fact that the government of Canada and the taxpayers of our country have in past years spent a great deal of money in making certain investigations and in bringing forward certain reports. I should like to draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, that for a period of almost three years there was a joint committee of the other place and the House of Commons on the subject of capital and corporal punishment and lotteries. On July 31, 1956, this joint committee submitted its report. There are many matters in that report which are not only worthy of immediate consideration, but should have immediate consideration because the House of Commons and the other place saw fit to request that certain matters be investigated.
There is also a report from a committee appointed to inquire into the principles and procedure followed in the remission service of the Department of Justice. This report is now known and recognized throughout Canada as the Fauteux report, and it was filed on April 30, 1956. Under the preceding administration, the House of Commons was given to understand that upon the filing of these reports the government would proceed to send copies to the attorneys general of the provinces and call an immediate conference with a view to getting agreement, so far as possible, upon enacting the necessary legislation. I believe it was either in the latter part of November or the early part of December, 1956, that a meeting was held in Ottawa, not of the attorneys general but of the heads of the departments who were sent here by the attorneys general for the

purpose of discussing these reports. I am sorry to say that as a result of only a one-day meeting-I think I am correct in making that statement-it was the decision of all those present that more information would have to be obtained; that they would report to the provinces and then be in a position to come back to Ottawa with their attorneys general and reach a decision.
As I said before, I think I am correct in stating that that meeting was held in the latter part of November or early in December of 1956. No meeting whatever was held in 1957, either by the departmental heads or the attorneys general. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that a couple of days ago I asked the Minister of Justice a question on orders of the day as to whether any date had been set for a conference of the attorneys general or departmental heads on these reports. The minister said no. This was a great disappointment to me, not only because of the time spent by the members of the other place and this house, as well as departmental officials, on these reports, but because of the importance of these reports. I was disappointed when the minister said only two or three days ago that it has not yet been possible to set a definite date for collaboration and discussion with the provinces on the implementation of some of the recommendations in the report which were filed, so far as the joint committee on capital and corporal punishment is concerned, on July 31 and the Fauteux report on April 30, 1956.
As I said, because I have two bills, one for second reading and one under notice, I am not going to deal specifically with the joint committee report of the other place and the House of Commons. However, I should like to draw the attention of the house to what I consider to be a most important and valuable report, namely what is known as the Fauteux report.
It has been my privilege to be a member of this house for not quite five years but to have been in parliament here and in the British Columbia legislature for almost 25 years. I consider this to be one of the finest reports that has ever been made on the question of penology. I am of opinion that it is one of the finest analyses ever made. I believe its recommendations are of such a nature that they should not be left in abeyance. I admit that there are some 44 recommendations in the report. I am convinced that a number of them could have been put into effect immediately in this House of Commons because they come completely within the purview and the jurisdiction of the federal house. Because my time is limited, because I believe the report is of
Supply-J ustice
such great importance, and because I regret so much that the Minister of Justice has informed us this week that there is still no date set for meeting with the attorneys general of the provinces, I should like briefly just to go over the recommendations and, merely by reading them, to explain thereby the importance of speedy action. If we go to page 87 of the report we find recommendation 2 which reads as follows:
2. Some means should he found whereby the courts, at all levels, may be made more conscious that the true purpose of punishment is the correction of the offender and not mere retribution by society.
That is one of the finest statements ever made. I believe it costs us about $4.50 a day for every day we keep a man in jail. The answer given by the Fauteux report is correction of the offender. That is one reason why I regret that with this report having been filed on April 30, 1956, the minister just two days ago said that no date has yet been set for a conference with the attorneys general. Recommendation 4 reads as follows:
4. The parliament of Canada should give serious consideration to
(a)	the abolition of a number of the restrictions on the power of courts to suspend the passing of sentence: and
(b)	the enactment of legislation to authorize probation without conviction.
That is something that is completely, wholly and solely within the power of the Minister of Justice and the federal government, on recommendation to this House of Commons and the other place.
Recommendation 7 reads as follows:
7. In passing sentences the court should rely, to a much greater extent than they now do, upon pre-sentence reports.
That is something that I would have hoped would be in effect by now. I am going to be obliged to jump over a number of recommendations. I should like to deal with all 44 of them but I am not going to be able to do so. I am going to jump to No. 16 which reads as follows:
16. Appropriate legislative amendments should be made immediately to provide that no person under the age of sixteen years shall be committed to penal institutions where adult prisoners are conSned.
That is being done now and has been done inside the last six weeks on convictions under our Criminal Code. I do not need to add to that. I can see my friend the Minister of Justice nodding his head. That is something that should have been into effect before now, namely that nobody under the age of 16 could be sent to an institution where adult criminals

are confined. I should like the minister to note recommendation 18 which reads:
18. Some means should be devised by which unjustified inequalities in the length of sentences of imprisonment, especially in the cases of cooffenders, can be remedied.
Perhaps it will be recalled that about six weeks ago, on the orders of the day, I asked the minister a question on that matter. Since that time I have acquired a great deal more evidence but I think it is important. We administer justice, but in the administration of justice it is important that those to whom we administer justice because they committed an offence should not feel that they have suffered an injustice. I have here reports from papers. I will give you one with regard to two men who committed the offence of breaking and entering on ten occasions, both together. One was given a suspended sentence on the ten charges of breaking and entering and the other one who was with him received a sentence of five years. I am not going to repeat what I said on the orders of the day with regard to matters of attempted rape and rape where under absolutely similar circumstances there have been terrific differences in the sentences. I believe the Fauteux report is very wise in making this recommendation which I have just quoted.
Mr. Chairman, I am trying to mention only the things which I feel are being too long delayed and which are still going to be delayed we do not know how long because of the answer of the minister that no date has been set for a conference between his department and the provinces. Because my time is as short as it is, I want to jump to recommendation 38 in the Fauteux report. It reads as follows:
38. Some means should be found to provide specialized after-care for particular types of parolees, such as sex offenders, drug addicts, alcoholics and psychopaths.
That brings me, in my remaining time, to a matter in which I have been interested for a great many years and I look forward to a statement from the minister upon it. I refer to the situation with regard to our drug addicts and the narcotic situation in Canada. I have been interested in this matter for a great many years. I am convinced that the governments of Canada should hang their heads in shame because we have never faced up to the situation and tried to do something of a constructive nature about it. I do want to say, however, that a start has been made in British Columbia and I hope the experiment is successful but on a national basis we have not done very much about the situation.
I hold in my hands the report of the United Nations commission on narcotic drugs. It is a summary of the annual reports and it gives

the situation across the world. May I refer the Minister of Justice to the part concerning Canada, according to the information given to this commission. It says this:
It is estimated that there are approximately
5.000	addicts who can he classified in the following groups:
(a)	Medical addicts consisting of individuals who, for medical reasons, have had narcotics prescribed in the course of treatment and who later on have not been able to forego completely this support, even though the medical condition was no longer a factor.
(b)	Professional people such as physicians, nurses, pharmacists, etc., with neurotic tendencies and easy access to narcotics, who have taken to narcotics as a "crutch".
(c)	Addicts obtaining drugs from illicit sources who become addicts through association with criminal elements or because of psychotic tendencies. These addicts usually do in fact obtain their drugs from illicit sources, although they occasionally prey upon physicians for drugs if illicit supplies become scarce.
Mr. Chairman, I want to read the final sentence in this United Nations report on Canada. It says:
No definite program of treatment for addicts has been formulated.
That is the report of Canada to this commission of the United Nations on narcotic drugs, that no definite program of treatment for addicts has been formulated although according to Canada's own report there are
5.000	admitted addicts in our own country.
I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the different picture in some other countries. Israel:	10 addicts were apprehended of whom 2 were physicians, etc. Norway: the number of drug addicts is estimated to be 300 to 400 practically all of whom are receiving drugs on a prescription. Poland: drug addiction is not a serious problem in that country; drug addicts are placed under the care of provincial mental health centres which direct them to psychiatric clinics for disintoxication treatment.
Then with respect to the United Kingdom, and I am still quoting from the United Nations report, the number of addicts receiving drugs from medical sources during the year was estimated to be 290. I believe our population in Canada is around 16 million and in the United Kingdom it is around 45 million. The United Kingdom says the number of addicts receiving drugs from medical sources is 290. There is no compulsory treatment for addicts and there are no state institutions specializing in the problems of addiction. There are, however, a number of public hospitals where treatment can be obtained and several private nursing homes dealing almost exclusively with alcoholics and drug addicts.

I could go from country to country but I will not do so because 1 am certain the Minister of Justice has an interest in this matter. I do want to say, however, that we in Canada are derelict in our responsibility in the handling of the narcotic problem. The way to start handling the narcotic problem is to take the profit away from those who make it by selling to the addicts.
The first way we can do that is to make sure that those who are addicts are treated as sick people and not as criminals. I am not a sentimentalist with respect to those who sell to addicts. They can be put in jail as far as I am concerned; put them in jail for life, but the addicts are sick people. If we on a national basis find some system- I do not say I know the answer-of treating addicts as sick people, enabling them to have treatment and to be registered, we can thereby take the profit out of the illicit trade in narcotics. That is the first step but I want to say more than that.
My late father and I have been most interested in this question and I could tell the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, of case after case about which I have personal knowledge. You will understand why I will not give names, but I know of case after case of drug addicts who eventually became criminals and who, time after time, went to Oakalla or to penitentiary because they had to steal in order to take care of their craving. I could also tell the minister of cases-plenty of them-where we finally got doctors, not only to take them under treatment but, because they had to have something all the time, to bring them down to a minimum and give them a dosage every day. Not one of them has ever gone back to jail since. I repeat, not one of them has gone back to jail since.
Is it not time that something was done? It is admitted that we have over 5,000 addicts in Canada. We in British Columbia are most concerned because according to all reports between one-half and one-third are in our province. Why I do not know but they are. Although a preliminary step has been taken in British Columbia by the provincial government and the committees which are now working in Vancouver and in the province with the government on a national basis, we should now admit how disgraceful it is that in the United Nations report we find the words I quoted a few moments ago.
There is no definite program of treatment for addicts; none has been formulated. Mr. Chairman, when the present Minister of Justice was on the other side of the house he was keenly interested in this matter. I remember that shortly before his election,
Supply-Justice
and shortly before he became the minister he said something was going to be done about this narcotic situation. So Mr. Chairman, I am asking the Minister of Justice through you if he will tell us why from July 31, 1956 to the present time there has been no meeting called to deal with this matter.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate very much what the hon. member for Vancouver East has said. I, too, am familiar with that report because I have been interested in this matter for a good many years, actively since 1908 and for ten years prior to that. I must say that since I came down here I have had great help from each of the ministers of justice. I remember well the first time when I placed a cash before the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. The big fellow just gave me a look: "Why do you want him out?" I said: "Because he is a human being and because I think he will make good." We got him out.
The reason I am on my feet now is because I want to say a word on behalf of those who are allowed out on parole or permit. I have had to deal with 107 cases. Today I have had one, through the kindness of Mr. MacLeod of the parole board, and out of all those cases there have been only three that went wrong. One was because of drink, another was because the man's wife was drinking and he did not have enough money to keep her going, and the other man, the son of a lord of Yorkshire, drank too. But the man who had a wife who was not worthy of him made good later; he went overseas and covered himself with honour.
Mr. Chairman, I can remember the first time I spoke to the present Leader of the Opposition with regard to criminals completing their sentences. He agreed that it was far better not to compel a prisoner to complete his sentence when it was not necessary, and I think the present Minister of Justice would be inclined to think that way, too. Why do these people go wrong? Most of them are young people. If you want to find a cure you must find the cause, and in my experience the worst cause is the liquor business. But many members of parliament, you know, are scared stiff of saying a word against the liquor business because there are so many votes involved. I pity the men who are in that position. I have never been in that position yet, and I never will. I believe that today no less than $965 millions are spent each year on liquor. The Minister of Justice should keep an eye on this business because it is the worse cause of crime we have in Canada today.
With regard to the present parole system, Mr. Chairman, one great need is that when

Supply-Justice
a young man, or any man for that matter, gets out he should find somebody ready to take an interest in him, because it is well known that so many of these men feel that nobody cares. "Who cares for me?" they ask. I am interested, now, in the case of a man at Fort William who has been in jail off and on for 15 years. I think he is improving because he has quit the drink. As I say, when these people get out on parole it is important they should find somebody who will take an interest in them, not for the sake of getting anything out of them but for the sake of helping them and enabling them to measure up and become good men and women.
We should line them up with some church -with whatever branch of the church they lean toward-and get the minister or priest, or somebody belonging to the church, interested in them and helping them to get back. This in my view is far better than leaving a man to his own devices on release. If a man feels that when he has served half his sentence someone will be interested in his case he has a great deal to look forward to and encourage him while he is in prison. Of course, it is not possible to get a man out until he has served half his sentence, at least that is my experience. It is only in special cases when something has gone wrong in the courts that there can be earlier release on parole. But when a man has served half his sentence, if someone is interested he can begin to have some hope. The real aim, in every case, is to help these men and women to measure up and become good Christians in practice.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words concerning judicial appointments. This is a matter of concern in British Columbia at the present time as we have vacancies in our hard working supreme court, which is the trial division, as well as on the court of appeal. In addition, notice has been given that this parliament will be asked to provide for two additional judges on the court of appeal of British Columbia. It is important if we are to have a strong, independent, imaginative judiciary that we attract the best people possible to this field of public service.
I begin by expressing the hope that the minister will not rule out candidates for the judiciary because they have taken part in party politics. Perhaps I should add that this is not a bid on my own part for a seat on the bench. I much prefer to take part in a fight rather than to preside over one. But politics is not a dirty word and should continue to attract in increasing measure
[Mr. Mclvor.l
many of those professional people who may later prove to be the best possible material for the judiciary. If their politics have been open, rather than of the back room strategy kind, so much more to their credit. The point is that the minister should draw upon all sources, regardless of what politics have been involved in the past, in order to get the best men. Just because we have a Conservative government should not mean that candidates for the judiciary must have had past Conservative leanings.
Then, too, judicial appointments should reflect the recommendations of the bar association of the province. Not that these recommendations should be considered binding, in my view, but the government should consult with these associations through their proper officers and give their recommendations most careful consideration. After all, working lawyers should have the best possible means of knowing who would and who would not make a good judge.
There is another point, however. While a judge may have had a political past it is important not only that he abandon politics on his elevation to the bench but that he should not have or seem to have a political future. Many of us regret the loss through resignation in the last few weeks of the services of the chief justice of British Columbia. Mr. Sloan made a noteworthy contribution as chief justice of the province. However, his services were bid for by the provincial government on a very handsome scale. The offer accepted was a ten-year contract with the provincial government at $50,000 a year for services which still remain rather vague.
We lose judges on occasion when they resign to go into private practice or into private business. That is one thing; but I deplore the action of a government in bidding for the services of prominent judges for work which, in this case, has inevitable political undertones. Indeed, it has even been suggested that the provincial government in this case was looking for a disinfectant for some of the political meat that has been allowed to rot in the attorney general's refrigerator. I therefore express the hope that this matter of bidding for the services of judges will not become a common practice because in a subtle but nonetheless marked manner it is bound to affect and undermine the strength and independence of the judiciary.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to continue with my previous remarks which will be of a brief nature and follow up what I had to say concerning the illicit narcotics situation in Canada. On occasion we read in the newspapers of the excellent work being done by

the undercover men of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and by local law enforcement officers in running down drug addicts and peddlers but it does not appear to have any visible effect in decreasing the traffic in drugs or improving the situation. As a matter of fact I have discussed this matter on more than one occasion with the law enforcement officers of the city of Vancouver. I have told them that I have known of a certain location in Vancouver where drug peddling is taking place and they have confirmed that I was correct. 1 then asked, "Why do you not step in and stop it?" The answer has been, "Because at that spot we know where to pick up the men we want to apprehend." This is not a healthy situation in my view.
Some 18 months ago a committee of the other place investigated the illicit narcotics situation and made a report with which I do not agree. As a matter of fact I think it was a stupid report. To the best of my knowledge the report has never been considered or discussed. The point I wish to emphasize and again draw to the attention of the minister is that we can say what we like about what is called the English system but nevertheless the facts are conclusive that in the United Kingdom, Israel, the Scandinavian and other countries where they recognize drug addiction as a sickness and register and treat addicts, and in cases where they cannot be cured allow the addicts to have the minimum dosage legally according to a physician's prescription, there is no narcotics problem. I have only to refer you, Mr. Chairman, and hon. members of this committee and the minister to the report of the United Nations committee to verify what I have said.
Why can we not face up to the situation in Canada and do something about the fact that, to the best of my knowledge, ours is the only country with a population of 16 million that has 5,000 drug addicts. Speaking of countries on this side of the iron curtain, because I have no knowledge of the situation on the other side, the majority of countries handle the problem in a practical, medical and scientific manner.
I want to repeat my position with regard to this matter because I have been misquoted on previous occasions. So far as those who peddle drugs are concerned the harshest penalty is not too harsh in my view excluding sentence of death, but with regard to addicts let us approach the problem from the standpoint of health, treating them as sick people rather than as criminals. My own experience has proven that if addicts are treated in that manner they can be rehabilitated and become useful citizens.
Supply-Justice
I should like now to refer to the Fauteux report. I have long been interested in the question of penology. I agree completely with the statement made by the Fauteux commission that we have to place more emphasis on correction and less on punitive sentences. The longer we delay in taking this action the more it will cost the taxpayers in keeping criminals in jail and the longer we will withhold making socially useful members of society of those who were previously antisocial. I was most interested in those sections of the report that dealt with the young offender and was particularly interested in the recommendation to the effect that judges should have a pre-sentence report and that probation should be given a high priority even before a sentence to jail. I admit that this is a very complex question. I wish to draw to the attention of the Minister of Justice section 32 of the report which says:
If it is not possible to implement these recommendations, or most of them, within the next two or three years, amendments should be made immediately to the Ticket of Leave Act as suggested in chapter VII of this report.
The two years are not yet over, because the report is dated April 30, 1956. I would draw the minister's attention to section 32, which apparently the commissioner and his colleagues felt to be of such importance that they said:
If it is not possible to implement these recommendations, or most of them, within the next two or three years, amendments should be made immediately to the Ticket of Leave Act as suggested in chapter VII of this report.
That has to do with the question of ticket of leave and parole. I would ask that the minister give this his attention. I could go on. This is a subject that is dear to my heart because I believe a great deal of good work can be done; but I think I have said enough to indicate to the minister what I have in mind. Perhaps for the first time he can give us the policy outlook of himself and his government and some assurance as to when he contemplates some action of a combined federal-provincial nature and in particular, sir, action on those things that come completely within the purview of the federal government. I hope he will take action on a federal basis in the near future if he is here.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to say how very much I am aware of and how very deeply I appreciate the fact that I am here tonight introducing the estimates of the Department of Justice for the first time as Minister of Justice. I want to take this occasion to express to my colleagues in the committee my appreciation of the very kind remarks they have made to me, both privately and publicly, on

Supply-Justice
the occasion of my appointment, and to tell them that I am fully aware of the fact that I follow a long line of most distinguished Canadians in what I regard as the finest appointment in the parliament of Canada.
In the office in the Justice building in which I carry on my work there hangs a photograph of the first minister of justice of Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald, and the long line of distinguished ministers carries on down through a list of names which are part of the warp and woof of Canadian history. Amongst them are members of both major parties, and not far from the end of the present line is the photograph of the honorary life president of the Canadian bar association, the Leader of the Opposition.
I know, sir, that I am not particularly called upon-and I am not capable of doing so if I were called upon-to say too much on this occasion but I find it appropriate, and I feel it appropriate, and I think my colleagues will feel it appropriate, if I pay tribute to a great lawyer and a great Canadian who retires shortly from his role as leader of his party and thus from the role of one who has contributed most actively and most splendidly to the public life of Canada.
It is in a consciousness of the tradition that I follow that I am grateful to my colleagues for the kind things they have said about me and the support they have given me in the role to which I have been summoned. I realize that there will come a time, there is bound to come a time, when controversy will, shall I say, displace the kind things that have been said but that is part of the life of parliament.

The
minister would like it that way, no doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But tonight I am introducing the estimates of the department and I should like to deal as best I can with the points which have been made by the speakers who have spoken in a general way on the first item. Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver East will forgive me if I reply to him in rather general terms on the basis that we can have a detailed discussion on the particular items when we reach them.
His main concern was with two subjects, namely the implementation of the Fauteux report and the question of reforms in the realm of the enforcement of the narcotic laws. My hon. friend found it a matter of criticism-I do not in any way resent his criticism-that no meetings had been held between representatives of this department and the attorneys general of the provinces or their representatives since this government had taken office. It is true that there has been no formal meeting, but I can tell him

that there were informal discussions with most of the attorneys general at the meeting of the Canadian bar association in Banff in September of last year, at which time I outlined in general terms, as I have outlined to the house since then, the method of procedure which we felt should be followed in connection with the Fauteux report.
The hon. member did refer to the fact that a meeting had been held in Ottawa in November, 1956, between the senior officials of the federal and provincial governments. I do not wish to make any disparaging remarks, but perhaps I can best summarize the situation by saying that nothing much was done between that meeting in November and the election which took place in June last year. After all, I am sure he will realize that the attention of the ministers of the previous government was engaged for some months prior to the actual date of the election upon the election campaign, and in that atmosphere it is probable that meetings for this purpose were not very easy to arrange.
However that may be, we found that when we took office there was nothing very concrete at hand in the department by way of proposals for the implementation of the report. Therefore, we in the department were faced with the necessity of deciding upon our course of action with regard to the problems with which the report confronted us. It seemed to me that the best and most sensible method of approach would be for us to make an assessment of the physical and financial implications involved in the Fauteux committee's recommendations because they are many and they are far-reaching; and that, having made that assessment, I would then seek from my colleagues in the government approval in principle of a method of approach. Having obtained that approval, I would then meet with the attorneys general of the provinces, or with their representatives, and ask them for their views as to whether the outline which we had been able to work out was acceptable or whether they wanted to modify it, and, if so, in what particulars.
We have therefore, been working in the department. We have assigned an officer to work exclusively on the recommendations of the Fauteux committee. I expect within a matter of a week or so to be able to lay before my colleagues in cabinet a report with recommendations as to what it seems we should do, and what we can do, with regard to the implementation of the Fauteux report, both in fields which are at present exclusively federal responsibility and fields which are joint responsibility. Having, as I say, obtained that approval in principle, then we would meet with the attorneys general of the provinces.

This approach has been communicated to the provincial representatives and they have indicated to me that they are in general agreement that that will be a sound and sensible method of approaching the problem. In the meantime, however, I quite agree with the hon. member, and with others who have spoken to me and written to me, that there are certain areas in what is presently the field of exclusive federal responsibility in which the Fauteux commission makes recommendations and in which we may proceed to implement some of those recommendations. Although we have not yet had a meeting, I am able to assure my hon. friend and the house that we have taken action on an appreciable number of these subjects.
For instance, one recommendation of the committee is that there is a great need for the immediate expansion of the regional services of the remission service. I should say, incidentally, that this is a matter entirely within the responsibility of this government and this parliament. I am glad to be able to report that in line with this recommendation we opened regional offices in Winnipeg, Toronto and Moncton in April of last year. A further office was opened in Kingston in July. Offices had previously been established at Montreal and Vanouver.
Another recommendation was that as soon as possible a system of automatic parole review should be instituted for Canada. I may say that this was a recommendation to which my hon. friend attached considerable importance. It was recommended that this automatic parole review should be instituted thereby dispensing with the system for requiring applications for parole. A system of automatic parole review has been started in three out of the eight Canadian penitentiaries. The system of automatic parole procedure that has been developed in respect of the inmates at these three institutions will, as quickly as circumstances permit, be extended to the remaining penitentiaries.
Another recommendation was that the annual conference of after-care agencies and government services should be continued in the future. Arrangements are being made for the holding of such a conference on a regional basis early in 1958.
Another recommendation was that parliament should give serious consideration to the abolition of the power of the courts to suspend the passing of sentence and the enactment of legislation to authorize probation without conviction. This is another of the steps referred to by my friend.

You have not moved on that one?
