I shall come to that in a
moment. Another recommendation was that the provisions of the criminal law that authorize imprisonment in default of payment of fines by persons who are unable to pay them should be repealed and that no distinction should be made in the law as far as time for payment of fines is concerned between indictable offences and summary conviction offences. My hon. friend went on to deal with a number of other recommendations of the commission involving changes in the system of administration of penitentiaries which would necessitate changes in the Criminal Code itself. The last recommendation to which I have just referred is one of those.
Again, while we have not had a meeting, we have been working on this matter in the department. I have before me now a number of specific recommendations for consideration involving, if they are approved, amendments to the criminal law, many of them arising out of the recommendations of the Fauteux commission. There are, I should think, some 15 or 20 of these recommendations which it has not been possible to deal with at this session, but which it is my hope we will be able to deal with or we will be able to incorporate into a bill to amend the Criminal Code which will be presented to parliament at its next session.
In these ways, Mr. Chairman, I can assure my hon. friend that although we have not had this meeting with the attorneys general of the provinces we expect to have it within the reasonably near future. In the other fields where we have exclusive responsibility we have been taking the necessary action and making the necessary study to be able to lay before parliament a comprehensive program with regard to the implementation of the Fauteux commission recommendation. We cannot do that at this session. These are a few specific things we can do, but action on many of the recommendations will have to wait probably until the next session.
My hon. friend referred to the question of narcotics and the problems of narcotic drugs. He referred to a report of the United Nations committee in which it is stated that there are some 5,000 addicts in Canada. No one can be happy that there are 5,000 addicts in Canada, whether or not those facts are accurate. The fact that we have this number of addicts, as compared with other countries with larger populations, is not a matter about which any person or any government or anybody in authority can be happy. My colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and I have had some preliminary discussions already. There are a number of conflicting views. The hon. member for Vancouver East, has said that he does not agree

Supply-Justice
with the report of the Senate committee. There have been other reports on this matter and other parties disagree with those reports. It is going to take some considerable time to try to sift through and analyse the different opinions that have been expressed by experts in the field and arrive at the best course of action to deal with this very pressing problem.
Are you going to do something?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are working on it now. My hon. friend has expressed the view that one approach might be to proceed against the peddlers and treat the addicts. I must confess that on the face of it that makes common-sense to me as a basis of approach, to punish most severely those who make a profit out of distributing and selling drugs and try to do something to treat and rehabilitate those who have been victimized by those terrible people who are prepared to make a profit out of the depravity of their fellow Canadians. I can assure my hon. friend we are just as seized with the importance of the subject as he is. If I seem to make excuses it is not because I am trying to hide behind the difficulty but because I want to assure him and the committee that when we move on it we want to move on a sound basis. That is the only reason we have not yet moved, because we are trying to study this problem and arrive at the best method of procedure.
I was grateful indeed to the tribute paid by the hon. member for Fort William to the staff of the remission service. In the short time that I have been serving as minister of this department I have found that there is no department of government better served than the Department of Justice. I want to pay my tribute to that department, and through them to all the civil servants with whom I have had the privilege of coming in contact in my capacity as minister since my appointment on June 21.
I can assure the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Kingsway that we will bear in mind the principles which he has suggested we should follow in the matter of judicial appointments.

At this time, Mr. Chairman, I should like to extend my personal congratulations to the Minister of Justice upon his appointment, and his further appointment as Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way spoke in the house this evening and mentioned that the selection of judges should be on a non-partisan basis. With that statement of fact I should like to agree with him.
But I say that it was very unfair of the hon. member to mention that there was a

political undertone in so far as the appointment of the Hon. Mr. Justice Sloan as the forestry chief in the province of British Columbia is concerned. Many of us know that Mr. Justice Sloan was in politics a Liberal and that fact certainly negatives any idea that there was a political undertone to his appointment. I would say that the Social Credit government in British Columbia made an excellent choice in picking him for the position he now holds. The Hon. Mr. Justice Sloan is recognized as one of the ablest men in western Canada if not in the whole of Canada. As far as I am personally concerned, I feel that the choice was a most excellent one. The Social Credit government of British Columbia did not draw any political line whatsoever. It went out to get the best man to serve a specific need in the province of British Columbia and the choice was a good one.
What has that to do with the estimates of the Department of Justice?

It has a great deal to do with them. This issue was raised in the House of Commons. The hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway brought this matter before the house and I am going to see that the statement is not unchallenged. I would also like to say this. I should like the Minister of Justice to give the following matter consideration. Many people say that the Hon. Mr. Justice Sloan is being paid $50,000 a year and that the amount is excessive. It is not the sum of $50,000 that is the important thing. The important thing is what the hon. gentleman takes home at the end of each and every month. Hon. members know what taxation is in this country today. They know that he takes home only a portion of that total amount.
In so far as our supreme court and county court judges in Canada today, are concerned, my understanding is that our supreme court judges are paid the sum of $16,900 a year and that our county court judges are paid $10,500. If we wish to have the finest legal brains in our country grace the bench and contribute their services to the public an inducement must be offered to attract those men to honourable positions in the country. I personally feel that our supreme court judges and our county court judges are not paid sufficient remuneration at the present time. It is my opinion that the amount they receive annually should be increased.
I read in the paper recently that the Hon. Mr. Justice Clyne, formerly of the supreme court of British Columbia has resigned in order to go into a field of business or economic activity. It could be the fact-although I am not saying that it is-that he will receive

greater financial reward elsewhere. I think as Canadians we should remember that our courts in this country are the last vestige of freedom. My opinion is that our judges should be paid a reasonable and proper amount. They are well worth it. I realize how hard these men work from day to day and the great responsibilities they assume.

I should like to make a comment or two in support of some of the remarks that have already been made about some of the activities under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice. They also have to do with drug addiction. I raise these matters, not in order to delay the progress of these estimates under this minister's department but in order to add a little bit of extra weight, if I can do so, to the comments already expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver East with respect to people who are addicted to drugs.
In my opinion the general public have a great misconception about people who are drug addicts. Until such time as we can overcome some of that misconception in the minds of the general public and probably in the minds of some of the members of this house I am convinced we shall have less chance of approaching the question of drug addiction in a sensible manner. There are probably five or six people who are at present members of the House of Commons who could be in possession of narcotics, and it would be perfectly all right. There is nothing illegal about that. They could not be convicted of possession as might many other individuals. I am referring to members of the legal profession.

You mean the medical
profession.

I mean the medical profession. I have some thoughts about the members of the legal profession but I expect I should not express them. It is perfectly all right for doctors to be in possession of narcotics and in fact is all right for some of them to be addicts, if they so desire, and maybe some of them are. I do not know. Certainly statistics show that in England there are medical doctors who are addicted to morphine and some of the other drugs. Here in Canada they can be addicted also. Yet society does not look down on them and the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act does not say that, because they are addicts they should be hauled up in court charged with possession and, if found guilty, sentenced to so many years in the penitentiary.
A number of people also have the misconception that people who are drug addicts are depraved in some way, that their mental
Supply-Justice
faculties are affected to the point where they must go out and steal, and that they are not fully in control of their abilities and of their mental faculties. To people who have that thought I think we should attempt to point out that it is a misconception. While I have been in public affairs for only a short period of time, nevertheless I have also taken an interest in drug addiction and in other related questions. I used to work out of an office which was situated on the corner of Hastings and Carroll streets in Vancouver and which, as the Minister of Justice will know as will others from Vancouver, is very close to a central hang-out of drug addicts, people who peddle drugs and push them and other people in the underworld. It is only about a block from there.
I have visited a couple of penal institutions under the jurisdiction of the federal government and have come to know a few people who are drug addicts. I have come to know them, although not personally or intimately, and have spoken to them about their addiction to drugs. All of them have substantially the same opinion and the same attitude. These people are addicted to drugs just in the same way as others might be addicted to alcohol or to nicotine. It is an addiction. The craving which they have, of course, is more serious and more compelling with narcotics than it is with nicotine or with alcohol.
When these people enter a penal institution, whether it be a provincial jail such as that at Oakalla or whether it be a federal penitentiary, they are given absolutely no assistance, guidance or treatment except that they are removed from the drug itself; they are not able to obtain drugs. As soon as they get back out again they still have a desire for it because of some psychological quirk or some glandular deficiency or some other reason. There is disagreement as to why people become drug addicts. But because they have this desire inside them, back they go to find out if they can get hold of some drugs again and back they are to addiction. So they enter a life of crime again, They have to shoplift, steal, break and enter, hold up, break into doctors' cars and elsewhere in order to get either the money to buy drugs on the illegal market or get the drugs themselves from whatever source they can get them. This is where they run into difficulty in more cases than by being in actual possession of the drugs.
I do hope that-I take the minister at his word-the study that is being given will be a deliberate and conscious study which will attempt to show to some of the other places in the world-and there are relatively few of them with an enlightened attitude towards

Supply-Justice
drug addicts and some program of treatment for them-that we also have an enlightened approach. I also hope, as I suspect has been the case in past years with some of the law enforcement officers, that we will not be guided by the attitude of the officials in the United States with respect to drug addiction. I understand there is a pretty fierce, backward and cruel approach there to people who are addicted to drugs and that we are following along somewhat the same lines which so far has solved nothing.
I have one or two instances I would like to give to the minister but he will probably want to indicate that these might more easily be dealt with under specific items. One of them relates to the public relations, or I should say the lack of them, of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It appears that in many cases officers of the R.C.M.P., many of them who are very youthful and in fact I understand there are some under the age of 21-

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member has invited my comment as to whether the subject to which he wishes to refer could be more properly dealt with elsewhere and I wonder if I could suggest to him that he wait until we reach item 396 under Royal Canadian Mounted Police on page 68 of the estimates.

Yes, it is very kind of the minister to indicate that. I do not know whether he would suggest that I should bring up the other item under some other vote, but it deals with the attitude of the courts. This is of course, under provincial jurisdiction in some cases because it relates more to magistrates court than to any others, but I have reference to the attitude of the courts and the chances which a native Indian gets in court when he is charged with almost anything. I know, having lived in an area where there are many native Indians for quite a while now, that many of them are not too conversant with the English language. I am sure the minister is aware of this fact but if there is a question asked with which they are not too familiar or if that question entails something they do not understand, their general reaction is to say "yes". I think anyone who knows anything about native Indians will agree that if they do not understand you they will say yes anyway and it takes a terrific amount of questioning or even cross-examination before you get to the real facts of the case-even when it is a matter for the Indian affairs branch-and to sift through all these "yesses" thrown at you.
What do you suggest should be done?
The solution would be to convince him to say, "no", I expect, or to plead not guilty to start with.

He
would probably say yes.

Whether the solution is a simple one which could be given in a few sentences is problematical but since the matter has been pin-pointed perhaps the minister will say it could be more properly dealt with under the Indian affairs branch, so that provision could be made to give the native Indian some sort of legal advice through that branch to ensure that his rights under our laws are protected to the fullest extent and to see that he gets the fairest possible treatment from the courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think in so far as this is a legal matter at all, it does fall under provincial jurisdiction and in so far as it is one dealing specifically with the administration of justice in the provinces, that should be dealt with in the same way. In so far as the question of the training of Indians and the protection of Indians when they get into courts is concerned it does to some extent fall under federal jurisdiction, but there it would come under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the estimates of which department I will be dealing with later.
I might just point out here that in capital cases the invariable practice is to provide Indians with legal assistance of the nature to which the hon. gentleman has referred.
I might add, Mr. Chairman, that these problems arise more particularly in magistrates' courts which are-

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Which are provincial courts exclusively.
No, I beg to differ-they are kangaroo courts.

I would like to ask a question of the Minister of Justice. When a man who has slipped a bit has been confined, are you in favour of giving him consideration by cancelling part of his sentence if he shows signs of making good?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think about the only answer I can give the hon. member is that I am very impressed with the work of the remission service. The principle upon which that service operates is that wherever the facts of the case indicate a prisoner can be successfully rehabilitated if discharged they go to work on such a basis. I am in full accord with that principle. Sometimes it does seem to some of us that they could work a little faster. On the other hand there are a great

many factors to be considered and in general I believe they work on a pretty sound basis.
Thank you.
Is the minister discussing now the remission branch or does he wish us to wait until item 173?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it suits the convenience of hon. members to move to item 173 that is perfectly satisfactory to me.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid it does not suit my convenience just now unless the minister can tell me that I am not dealing with that part of the estimates where the question I have in mind could be asked. I am faced with another difficulty. I wish the minister would occupy some other dual position than that of Minister of Justice and that of Minister of Citizenship and Immigration because I have questions in mind which may deal with both of those positions.
First of all, I want to bring the minister back to a question I asked last November about one Per Holting, a Canadian citizen who boarded a S.A.S. aircraft in Greenland, having purchased a ticket from there through to Los Angeles and when the plane touched down in Winnipeg, got off the plane. I agree that according to the ticket Mr. Holting should have gone right through to Los Angeles and I suppose it was part of the contract between Mr. Holting and S.A.S. that he should do so.
Nevertheless this Canadian citizen, having got off the plane at Winnipeg, decided he would like to break his journey permanently at that point. In an answer the minister gave to me he said that the police of St. James, at the request of the captain of the aircraft, literally had Mr. Holting put back on that plane, and I suppose it would have been done -no matter how gently-nevertheless forcibly.
I would like to know if it is possible for a Canadian citizen to be deported from this country in such a way and, if so, under what law? This man was sent out of his country. Here again there is the question as to whether this should come under the Department of Justice or under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, but I think there is an element of law in this matter, and I would like to know what the Minister has to say about what I call the deportation of Mr. Holting, a word which I gathered was disagreed with previously. The fact remains that a Canadian citizen was deported, sent out of this country by police officers, acting, I have no doubt, honestly. Nevertheless he was sent out of this country (to another land
Supply-Justice
and had to find his way back. I should like to find out under what law this man was exiled from Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think that part of the hon. gentleman's question might better be asked on the estimates of the Department of Transport which is responsible for questions arising under these international air agreements, and under which the particular air line in question was prohibited from allowing a passenger to deplane in Winnipeg.

Or the Department of
External Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I might almost say any department other than my own. I do assure the hon. gentleman that this department is not responsible in this matter at all. Mr. Holting was not arrested-perhaps I should say interfered with-by federal police; he was not interfered with by any officers of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Representations that were made to any authorities were made by the air line officials who were seeking to discharge the terms under which they were given the right to land in Winnipeg. The police involved in the case were, I believe, the St. James municipal police. Mr. Holting suffered himself to be led back to the plane, and went on to Los Angeles, and while I understand the apprehension and dissatisfaction felt by the hon. member I think that in the circumstances I must take the position, in dealing with the estimates of the Department of Justice, that there is nothing here for me to answer.

But is this not a matter which should be the concern of the Minister of Justice. Is it possible that under our system of law in this country a Canadian can be deported from Canada? Is there not a principle here? A Canadian lands here and surely, if he decided to stay, it would be the duty of the S.A.S. to take action against him and to do it properly through the courts. Is there not a violation of law here? What does the Minister of Justice have to say about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that if Mr. Holting feels that he was improperly treated a remedy would be open to him by way of whatever action he may see fit to take against those by whom he feels he was improperly treated. I do not think as Minister of Justice I should be drawn into expressing an opinion beyond the general statement I have made. The difficulty under which I labour is that as a private citizen I might be as much concerned about the situation as is the hon. member, but the moment I say something here as Minister

Supply-Justice
of Justice I might be taken as expressing an official opinion that Mr. Holting should or should not follow a certain course of action.
should direct a question to the minister in his capacity as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will I get the same answer, or will I get a fuller answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would depend entirely on the question which the hon. gentleman asks.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask a question with regard to item 172. I notice that the increase in this item is approximately $9,000. Would the minister like to report on what progress has been made in Canada in so far as uniformity of legislation is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The increase of $9,497 is for the entire departmental administration, whereas the amount voted to the Commissioners with respect to promoting uniformity of legislation is only $200, which is the amount actually expended this year. Their meeting took place in Calgary in September just prior to the meeting of the Canadian Bar Association.
What progress has been made in so far as uniformity of legislation is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is a matter which is
largely of concern to the provinces. What is sought in these meetings is to bring legislation and legal practices in the various provinces into conformity as far as is possible. Our interest as I understand it, is more a watching interest than a direct interest because of course when we legislate we legislate for the whole dominion.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question which, as he knows, has been directed to a number of his colleagues on the first item of their estimates. Is he making any reductions in the estimates of his department for this year, and has he found any examples of waste or extravagance?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I propose to move three reductions in the estimates, one in the combines branch-and I assure the hon. member that it does not represent any diminution in the work of that branch- one in the penitentiaries and one in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In so far as the other part of the question is concerned, that is to waste and extravagance, I do not recall

that when I sat on that side of the house I ever made any allegations of waste and extravagance against this particular department.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether, if this government gets down to attempting to bring the labour laws of Canada into conformity, that will be done under the system for promoting conformity of legislation dealt with in item 172.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I imagine that the discussion of labour legislation could take place at the meetings to which reference has been made, but it would be more likely to take place at a conference of labour ministers or deputy labour ministers, and I understand that such conferences do take place from time to time.
Does the uniformity referred to under this heading mean uniformity as to the substance of legislation or just uniformity as to the form?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not sure I heard the hon. member's question fully, but the sort of topic that would be discussed would be uniformity of highway legislation, uniformity with regard to bill of sale acts, mechanics liens acts and subjects of that nature. I am not sure whether that answers the hon. gentleman's question.

In
part. If I may repeat my question, I asked whether what was sought was uniformity as to substance or uniformity as to form.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The answer would be both.
What is it that limits the type of subjects that are considered? The field that has been mentioned is rather narrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I understand it there would be no limitations as to the type of subject. The subjects covered would be those suggested from time to time in correspondence between the various attorneys general. The hon. gentleman will recall that a couple of years ago we had extended discussions here on highways legislation; and it might be that as a result of such discussions it would be suggested to the committee that the highway codes of the various provinces should be discussed at the conference. There is I understand no limitation on the headings of legislation which might be discussed at the conference.

Mr. Chairman, on page 241 respecting the details of this particular item I notice that the bulk of the $9,497 increase

this year over last year results from an increase of salaries to the civil servants or to those responsible for administration. I note, too, that there are listed on that page an estimated 108 employees for 1957-58 as compared with 109 last year. I am not taking any exception to the increase in salaries, but I am wondering whether these 108 jobs are all filled at one time, or what percentage of them are ever filled.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in this department we have a staff turnover problem just as any other department of government or indeed any business employing a comparable number of personnel would have. The desire of the department and the effort of the administrators of the department is directed toward keeping the positions filled in so far as it is possible to do so because the efficient functioning of the department depends upon keeping the positions manned to as full an extent as possible.

Just by way of example, Mr. Chairman, we are estimating this year that we shall have three deputy assistants to the Minister of Justice at a salary of $15,000. We provided for three last year and I am wondering if we have the three each year. Did we have three last year? When did we last have three?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the answer to that question is mainly that up until May of 1957 Mr. F. P. Varcoe, Q.C. was deputy minister of justice. He then retired and Mr. W. R. Jackett, Q.C. who sits in front of me here was appointed deputy minister. Prior to his appointment we had three assistant deputy ministers. We now have only two and I am informed that in next year's estimates we will only have establishment for two assistant deputy ministers.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister one question of detail. Reference was made earlier this evening to the resignation from the bench of Mr. Justice Sloan. Can the minister say whether the pension which the governor in council may grant to a judge on retirement has been granted to Mr. Sloan for the period when he will be doing this other job at $50,000 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, no pension has as yet been granted to retired Chief Justice Sloan. The matter is by way of correspondence before me for consideration and I would not care to go further at the moment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Supply-Justice
173.	Remission service, including $40,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by treasury board, $267,835.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has stated that he is going to move for reduction of a couple of items but he did not mention this one and I am very glad he did not. As a matter of fact, although it is now only a matter of a few months before the estimates run out I want to say something on behalf of the remission service and express the hope that the minister, if not now at least in the future, will greatly increase the budget of this service.
It has been my experience since I came to Ottawa as the result of the election in 1953 to have to take up a number of cases with the remission service. I would direct the attention of the hon. members to the amount of money allocated to this branch. Quite bluntly, I must say I do not think the remission service can possibly do the job it is supposed to do or would want to do on this budget. It is the responsibility of the service to make up all the necessary documents for submission to the Solicitor General for the report to the governor general in council with regard to any person who is sentenced to death for homicide and who appeals the sentence. That is automatic. I also understand that those who have their death sentence commuted to life imprisonment have their sentence reviewed by the service after 12 years. There is also an automatic review in the case of all those who are committed to penitentiaries as habitual criminals or psychopaths. I believe this is done every three years after a definite period. The remission service also has to deal, if not on an automatic basis at least on request, with the question of appeals for parole and ticket of leave of every person in Canada who has been given a sentence of two years or more.
I am sorry that I do not have the record here of the number of cases the remission service is supposed to review on a complete and honest basis and on which it must make recommendations as to whether or not a parole should be granted. I notice that in the present estimates from the administrative viewpoint there is a staff increase of only three. As I said I know that the estimates will have run out in about two months but as one who has had considerable experience with the remission service I want to say that I believe they would be the first to admit that they are completely overworked. They do not have adequate staff to handle cases to the extent they should. I sincerely hope that the minister will see to it that there is a substantial increase in the estimates for this service in line with the recommendation of the Fauteux report in order to place the

Supply-Justice
service on the basis outlined in that report and also, I believe, in line with the thinking of the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have the advice of the hon. member. The increase this year as against the year before is not three but nine or nearly 20 per cent over last year.
It is only three in the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has increased from 46 to 55.
I am speaking about the administrative aspect. I am not including stenographers or others who are not involved in making decisions or doing research.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If you confine it to the administrative staff I am sure the percentage increase is even greater. I am glad to be able to assure my hon. friend that I expect to have before me within the next two weeks recommendations from the department with regard to the institution of a parole board along the lines of the recommendation of the Fauteux commission report which, of course, is all bound up with this report of the remission service. The matter of staff and the function and position of the board will be considered at the same time that that other matter is being considered.

I sincerely hope that when the change is being made the director of the remission service will be allocated to the job of directing the service only and will not have to take on any additional responsibilities.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question with regard to item No. 173. I notice that the sum of $40,000 is mentioned in there as grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, an increase of $10,000 over last year. Then, if we turn to item No. 182 on page 36 the sum of $60,000 is mentioned for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies which has been increased from the sum of $50,000 allocated last year. I recognize the good work that these societies are doing but I would like an explanation as to the increase and as to why these two items are separated one under the heading "Penitentiaries" and one under "Department".

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to the increase in item No. 182 perhaps the hon. gentleman would permit me to wait until we reach that item under "Penitentiaries" before dealing with it. Under item No. 173, the hon. gentleman will appreciate that these prisoners' aid societies do a great deal of the supervisory and reporting work on the prisoners released on parole or ticket of leave. As I announced earlier, we have established additional regional offices and it is the increases arising from such

developments which account for the increased work which is being undertaken for the department by these prisoners' aid societies. The hon. member will also agree-I think I am correct in saying this-that this is in line with the recommendation of the Fauteux committee that we should make every use possible of recognized prisoners' aid societies.
Will the minister indicate why we have two items?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member will appreciate that the prisoners aid societies do work while the prisoner is in the penitentiary at which time provision is made by the penitentiaries branch and after he leaves the penitentiary at which time provision is made under this item.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Exchequer Court of Canada-
175. Administration, $108,760.

Mr. Chairman, this item has to do with the administration of the Exchequer Court of Canada. Has the minister yet had time, with all the other responsibilities that are his since he is in charge of two departments, to give consideration to the idea that we have proposed in this house on a number of occasions, namely that the exchequer court might be asked to take on the handling of those divorces which are now being dealt with by parliament. Some of us are aware of the fact, although I was not personally involved, that 20 or 30 members of the House of Commons spent the greater part of this day hearing one divorce case. The information about that hearing that has been communicated to me makes me feel, as I am sure the minister does, that that is hardly the business for which members of parliament are elected. I am fully aware of the feelings that are aroused when one mentions this matter. I am aware of the arguments that are proposed against the suggestion that we have made. It does seem to me, however, that it is a way of getting divorces out of parliament and yet at the same time not establishing a divorce court in either of those provinces where it is not wanted.
As far as I am concerned, any alternative suggestion that would be better or more practicable would be equally welcomed. I wonder whether the minister, together with his officials, has given any consideration to this matter. If not, would he put it on his agenda?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, I have to confess to the hon. gentleman that it will be more a case of putting it on the agenda than being able

to report much progress. It seems to me the problem is, to use the word in its broader sense, more a political one than an administrative one and therefore I hesitate somewhat to put any onus on the department. I can only report that I have had some preliminary discussion with the Speaker of the other place, but I am not able to report that we have made much progress. I am as uneasy about the situation as is my hon. friend and I shall continue to try to work something out.
Knowing the readiness of my hon. friend to pursue matters about which he is uneasy, these words of his are very welcome.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the hon. member must not expect me to be a star gazer quite that far away. The business tomorrow will be the continuation of the estimates of justice and then fisheries and national revenue. On Saturday we shall continue with estimates. I am hoping that Monday will be a government day. There will be a notice of motion in Votes and Proceedings tomorrow dealing with Monday and I expect we shall have legislation on Monday and Tuesday but I cannot go any farther than that at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the house leader not able to say what will be taken up on Tuesday and Wednesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I cannot say that far ahead, Mr. Speaker. I will let the hon. member know just as soon as I can.

I was just wondering, Mr. Speaker, whether I might make a suggestion to the house leader. Everybody knows how important to the Liberals the coming convention is. Some of us may not think it is too important. They are shy. I never saw such a shy bunch of fellows in my life. Otherwise, I think they would have made a request for time off. Since they are shy, I do not mind suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that it does not hurt to be a bit chivalrous sometimes. I would suggest to the house leader that he give consideration to adjourning the house during the Liberal convention. I should like to see how they carry on, and perhaps get a pointer or two. I would strongly suggest that the house leader give consideration to that suggestion. I might just assure him that my group would be quite prepared to support him if he will propose that the house adjourn for the duration of the convention. We should go down and see for ourselves what effect the first epistle to the Babylonians is going to have. I do suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the house leader give that careful consideration.
